## pqac-00000014

From text 'fedina2022influenceofalsi10mg pages 5-6'.

Tatiana Fedina, Filippo Belelli, Giorgia Lupi, Benedikt Brandau, Riccardo Casati, Raphael Berneth, Frank Brueckner, and Alexander F.H. Kaplan. Influence of alsi10mg powder aging on the material degradation and its processing in laser powder bed fusion. Powder Technology, 412:118024, Nov 2022. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.powtec.2022.118024, doi:10.1016/j.powtec.2022.118024. This article has 27 citations and is from a domain leading peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt reports measured oxygen contents only for AlSi10Mg, not AlSi12. For fresh/virgin AlSi10Mg powder, oxygen was 0.067 wt% (±0.03). After processing, the R0 powder contained 0.072 wt% oxygen, indicating a slight increase. Powder aged for 96 h contained 0.257 wt% oxygen (±0.07), approximately four times the virgin value; this was attributed to oxidation during prolonged heat exposure in an active-gas atmosphere. Oxygen was measured using hot-gas extraction, and the 96 h condition was selected as the worst-case aging scenario. The excerpt mentions that aluminum alloys can absorb hydrogen during storage or aging, potentially promoting pore formation, but explicitly states that no direct tendency was observed in this study and gives no hydrogen concentration in ppm. It also does not provide humidity-controlled results, oxygen chamber concentration in ppm, LPBF porosity measurements, or powder-layer thickness. The reported before/after comparison concerns virgin powder, processed/R0 powder, and aged powder; processed powders were additionally sieved after LPBF, with an increased coarse fraction for aged material, likely due to oxygen-related melt-pool instability and spatter. Thus, oxygen wt% values are distinguishable from chamber oxygen ppm, but chamber ppm is not reported here.


---

## pqac-00000015

From text 'fedina2022influenceofalsi10mg pages 4-5'.

Tatiana Fedina, Filippo Belelli, Giorgia Lupi, Benedikt Brandau, Riccardo Casati, Raphael Berneth, Frank Brueckner, and Alexander F.H. Kaplan. Influence of alsi10mg powder aging on the material degradation and its processing in laser powder bed fusion. Powder Technology, 412:118024, Nov 2022. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.powtec.2022.118024, doi:10.1016/j.powtec.2022.118024. This article has 27 citations and is from a domain leading peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt provides measurements for AlSi10Mg, but not AlSi12. In Table 1, fresh/virgin AlSi10Mg contained 0.067 wt% oxygen and 0.003 wt% hydrogen, equivalent to approximately 30 ppm hydrogen. After 96 h aging, oxygen increased to 0.257 wt%, while hydrogen remained 0.003 wt% (approximately 30 ppm). The corresponding R0 condition measured 0.072 wt% oxygen and 0.003 wt% hydrogen before aging, increasing to 0.274 wt% oxygen and 0.004 wt% hydrogen (approximately 40 ppm) after 96 h. These are powder oxygen and hydrogen concentrations, not chamber-gas concentrations. During LPBF, argon maintained chamber oxygen below 1000 ppm. The process used a 50 μm powder layer thickness. The study compared virgin and aged powders in manufactured cubes and prisms, assessing density, microstructure, tensile properties, and porosity. CT was performed on R0 and R0-aged-96 h cubes at 10.5 μm spatial resolution, but the excerpt does not report the actual porosity values. It also does not provide a quantified humidity effect; it describes systematic aging via heat treatment and ambient-atmosphere degradation rather than a humidity-controlled comparison.

## pqac-00000016

From text 'fiegl2021effectofalsi10mg0.4 pages 1-2'.

Tobias Fiegl, Martin Franke, Ahmad Raza, Eduard Hryha, and Carolin Körner. Effect of alsi10mg0.4 long-term reused powder in pbf-lb/m on the mechanical properties. Materials & Design, 212:110176, Dec 2021. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.matdes.2021.110176, doi:10.1016/j.matdes.2021.110176. This article has 65 citations and is from a highest quality peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt reports that AlSi10Mg0.4 powder degradation increases oxygen and hydrogen contents and raises LPBF/PBF-LB/M porosity. Using process parameters qualified for virgin powder, porosity increased from below 1% to approximately 3% for long-term reused powder, while tensile and yield strength decreased by about 15%. The excerpt does not provide the actual measured powder oxygen values in wt% or hydrogen values in ppm for fresh versus aged AlSi10Mg powder. It also does not give a complete fresh/aged measurement table or specific numerical oxygen concentration in the powder. The approximately 1000 ppm value refers to oxygen in the protective process atmosphere/chamber, not oxygen wt% in the powder, and these quantities should be kept separate. For the cited Al-121Si experiment (potentially relevant to AlSi12, but the excerpt does not explicitly identify it as AlSi12), virgin powder stored for one month in ambient air produced about 3% porosity, whereas powder dried at 100 °C for one hour produced about 1%. This demonstrates a humidity/moisture effect: drying reduced moisture associated with oxide, carbonate-hydroxide, and water species and lowered porosity. The specimens used 50 µm powder layers and a 200 °C preheating temperature. Exact oxygen wt%, hydrogen ppm, and AlSi12-specific results require the full article or cited source.

## pqac-00000017

From text 'fiegl2021effectofalsi10mg0.4 pages 3-4'.

Tobias Fiegl, Martin Franke, Ahmad Raza, Eduard Hryha, and Carolin Körner. Effect of alsi10mg0.4 long-term reused powder in pbf-lb/m on the mechanical properties. Materials & Design, 212:110176, Dec 2021. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.matdes.2021.110176, doi:10.1016/j.matdes.2021.110176. This article has 65 citations and is from a highest quality peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt reports measurements only for AlSi10Mg; no AlSi12 data are provided. For fresh/virgin AlSi10Mg powder, oxygen content was approximately 0.05 wt% (described as 0.05%), while powder reused for more than 30 months had approximately 0.12 wt%, representing a doubling during recirculation. Hydrogen increased from 80 ppm in virgin powder to 130 ppm in the long-term reused powder. The excerpt does not report a humidity exposure or humidity-effect experiment, nor does it provide oxygen concentration in a process chamber in ppm; the oxygen values are powder oxygen measurements, distinct from chamber-gas measurements. Powder cross-section characterization found approximately 0.6–0.7% internal porosity in both powder conditions. For the LPBF tensile-specimen experiment, specimens were manufactured from virgin and long-term reused powder, and the text states that gas porosity dominated the resulting defects, with some larger lack-of-fusion defects occurring statistically. The process-parameter table lists a layer thickness of 100 (the extracted table heading says mm, although LPBF layer thickness is ordinarily reported in micrometres). The cited excerpt does not give a numerical measured LPBF bulk porosity value.

## pqac-00000018

From text 'fedina2022influenceofalsi10mg pages 2-4'.

Tatiana Fedina, Filippo Belelli, Giorgia Lupi, Benedikt Brandau, Riccardo Casati, Raphael Berneth, Frank Brueckner, and Alexander F.H. Kaplan. Influence of alsi10mg powder aging on the material degradation and its processing in laser powder bed fusion. Powder Technology, 412:118024, Nov 2022. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.powtec.2022.118024, doi:10.1016/j.powtec.2022.118024. This article has 27 citations and is from a domain leading peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt describes an AlSi10Mg study in which gas-atomized powder with a 20–63 μm size range was artificially aged in an open-atmosphere muffle furnace at 400 °C for 6, 12, 24, 48, and 96 hours. The treatment was intended to accelerate oxidation and simulate degradation associated with repeated laser processing. Chemical composition was measured by ICP-OES, silicon by gravimetry, and oxygen, nitrogen, and hydrogen by hot-gas extraction. However, this excerpt does not report the actual measured oxygen values in wt%, hydrogen values in ppm, or any comparison between fresh and aged powder. It also contains no AlSi12 data, no humidity-effect experiment, and no oxygen-chamber concentration reported in ppm; therefore, a distinction between powder oxygen wt% and chamber oxygen ppm cannot be established from the provided pages. LPBF processing was performed only for the R0 condition and the 96-hour aged powder after one processing cycle, with the latter designated the worst-case condition. Powder morphology and final-part porosity were examined using SEM and X-ray computed tomography, respectively, while porosity was calculated from relative density. The excerpt does not provide measured LPBF porosity results, before/after numerical comparisons, or the powder-layer thickness used in processing.

## pqac-00000019

From text 'fiegl2021effectofalsi10mg0.4 pages 2-3'.

Tobias Fiegl, Martin Franke, Ahmad Raza, Eduard Hryha, and Carolin Körner. Effect of alsi10mg0.4 long-term reused powder in pbf-lb/m on the mechanical properties. Materials & Design, 212:110176, Dec 2021. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.matdes.2021.110176, doi:10.1016/j.matdes.2021.110176. This article has 65 citations and is from a highest quality peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt concerns AlSi10Mg0.4 rather than AlSi12 and does not provide actual measured oxygen concentrations in wt% or hydrogen concentrations in ppm for fresh versus aged powder. It reports degradation indicators instead: after 30 months of reuse, sieved feedstock contained up to 3% spatter, spatter oxide scales reached approximately 125 nm, and the average oxide layer thickness increased from 4 nm for virgin powder to 38 nm for powder reused for 30 months. The cited humidity/drying experiment on virgin AlSi10Mg found that drying before melting reduced porosity from about 0.5% without drying to 0.4% after drying at 90 °C and 0.2% after drying at 200 °C. The mechanism described is moisture-related hydrogen generation in the aluminum melt, with lower hydrogen solubility in solid aluminum causing pores; moisture also reduces flowability through liquid bridges and agglomeration. The study’s LPBF system used continuous nitrogen flooding to limit oxidation, although slight leakage allowed oxygen contact. The excerpt states that the present work addressed 100 μm powder layers, but the detailed measured fresh/aged oxygen and hydrogen values and final LPBF porosity results are not included in these pages. No AlSi12 data, chamber oxygen ppm values, or before/after chamber measurements are provided.

## pqac-00000020

From text 'fedina2022influenceofalsi10mg pages 6-8'.

Tatiana Fedina, Filippo Belelli, Giorgia Lupi, Benedikt Brandau, Riccardo Casati, Raphael Berneth, Frank Brueckner, and Alexander F.H. Kaplan. Influence of alsi10mg powder aging on the material degradation and its processing in laser powder bed fusion. Powder Technology, 412:118024, Nov 2022. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.powtec.2022.118024, doi:10.1016/j.powtec.2022.118024. This article has 27 citations and is from a domain leading peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt provides partial information for AlSi10Mg, comparing virgin powder with R0 (processed/recovered) and powder aged for 96 h, including R0 aged 96 h. Aging promoted powder coarsening: D50 increased from 39.8 μm for virgin powder to 43.1 μm after 96 h aging, while R0 remained approximately unchanged. Aging was associated with oxide formation on particle surfaces, reduced laser absorbance, and possible agglomeration. At the 1070 nm fiber-laser wavelength, virgin and R0 absorbance were nearly unchanged, whereas aged powder showed substantially lower absorbance; the reported average absorbance fell from 68.55% for virgin powder to 58.23% for aged 96 h, described as a 15% decrease. LPBF parts made from R0 powder had 96.48 ± 0.22% relative density and 3.52% porosity, while R0 aged 96 h parts had 93.50 ± 0.41% relative density and 6.50% porosity. The excerpt does not provide actual oxygen concentrations in wt%, hydrogen concentrations in ppm, chamber oxygen in ppm, humidity effects, AlSi12 data, a separate distinction between powder oxygen and chamber oxygen, or powder-layer thickness. It also does not give a complete before/after experimental oxygen or hydrogen dataset; it only identifies virgin, processed/recovered, and 96-hour-aged powder states.

## pqac-00000021

From text 'raza2021degradationofalsi10mg pages 3-4'.

Ahmad Raza, Tobias Fiegl, Imran Hanif, Andreas MarkstrÖm, Martin Franke, Carolin Körner, and Eduard Hryha. Degradation of alsi10mg powder during laser based powder bed fusion processing. Materials & Design, 198:109358, Jan 2021. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.matdes.2020.109358, doi:10.1016/j.matdes.2020.109358. This article has 95 citations and is from a highest quality peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt concerns AlSi10Mg powder degradation during laser-based powder bed fusion (LB-PBF), comparing virgin powder (Al0) with powder reused for 6, 10, 14, and 30 months (Al6, Al10, Al14, and Al30). It reports that bulk oxygen content increased with reuse time, with a sharp increase between Al0 and Al6, followed by a slower increase after six months attributed to surface passivation and formation of a stable aluminum-oxide layer. The excerpt does not provide the numerical oxygen concentrations in wt%, hydrogen concentrations in ppm, chamber oxygen or humidity values, or measured LPBF porosity. It also does not compare AlSi10Mg with AlSi12. Particle-size distribution remained broadly consistent over time, which the authors associate with agglomerate removal during sieving, removal of fines by the processing atmosphere, and adhesion of fine particles to powder-system components. Fresh Al0 powder contained satellite particles, whereas multiply reused Al30 powder had a smoother surface and lacked satellites, attributed to repeated sieving and friction during transport. Stable Al2O3 and/or Al-Mg-oxide layers were identified as relevant oxidation products. The excerpt mentions powder layer thickness only in connection with XPS etch-depth/oxide-thickness analysis, without stating a numerical powder-layer thickness.

## pqac-00000022

From text 'bhowmick2007neardrymachiningof pages 139-142'.

S Bhowmick. Near-dry machining of 319 aluminum-silicon alloy. Unknown journal, 2007.

The excerpt reports aluminum transfer and adhesion to the drills during dry drilling of 319 aluminum alloy, but it does not provide a measured HSS flank-wear dimension, drill mass loss, tool-material transfer into the aluminum, or embedded abrasive-particle measurements. For the uncoated HSS drill, excessive aluminum adhered to both the cutting edge and drill flutes; the drill became stuck during the 49th hole, defining failure. The adhered aluminum mass after the 49th hole was reported as 342 x 10'3 gm (as written in the excerpt). The excerpt also states that aluminum adhesion fluctuated because aluminum was alternately built up and removed. For H-DLC-coated HSS, adhered aluminum after 150 holes was 3.6 x 10'3 gm, with no failure observed; the text characterizes this as nearly a 100% reduction relative to uncoated HSS and reports at least three times longer tool life. For NH-DLC-coated drills, adhered aluminum after 150 holes was 10.08 x 10'3 gm, with no failure for at least 150 holes. Thus, the reported built-up/adhesive material is explicitly aluminum, not tool metal, but the excerpt does not establish whether any tool material or abrasive particles became embedded in the workpiece.


---

## pqac-00000023

From text 'zhang2001wearmechanismmaps pages 4-5'.

M. Zhang, Yucheng Liu, and Hui Zhou. Wear mechanism maps of uncoated hss tools drilling die-cast aluminum alloy. Tribology International, 34:727-731, Nov 2001. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/s0301-679x(01)00058-5, doi:10.1016/s0301-679x(01)00058-5. This article has 43 citations and is from a domain leading peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt reports qualitative SEM observations of uncoated HSS drill flank wear during dry drilling of die-cast aluminum, rather than numerical flank-wear dimensions, drill mass loss, or quantified transfer volumes. At 200 mm/min feed and 4500 rev/min cutting speed, deeper parallel furrows and increased transferred aluminum indicate combined adhesive and abrasive wear. At 8000 rev/min, severe plastic distortion and plastic flow occur; deformed edges rupture and cracks form on the worn surface, attributed mainly to high tool–workpiece interface temperatures. At 10,000 rev/min, the worn surface has smooth matrix waves and carbide-particle islands resembling a river bottom. The authors identify thermal wear, including material transfer and diffusion, as the main mechanism at high speed/feed, with molten aluminum flow producing surface erosion and river-bottom-like patterns. Wear rises rapidly in this high-severity region, which should be avoided. The excerpt does not establish whether any built-up edge consists of aluminum versus tool metal, nor does it provide direct measurements of flank-wear width/depth, drill mass loss, transferred-material thickness, or embedded abrasive-particle concentration. It does, however, indicate aluminum transfer and the presence/exposure of carbide particles in the worn HSS surface.


---

## pqac-00000024

From text 'zhang2001wearmechanismmaps pages 2-4'.

M. Zhang, Yucheng Liu, and Hui Zhou. Wear mechanism maps of uncoated hss tools drilling die-cast aluminum alloy. Tribology International, 34:727-731, Nov 2001. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/s0301-679x(01)00058-5, doi:10.1016/s0301-679x(01)00058-5. This article has 43 citations and is from a domain leading peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt reports measured flank wear for uncoated HSS drilling tools during dry drilling of die-cast AlSi9Cu3. Wear was measured with a toolmaker’s microscope at 30× magnification and 100 µm accuracy. Figure 3 presents normalized flank-wear-rate values as log10(VB/L), with the lowest wear-rate region reported as approximately 7.30–7.60; the text also groups regions A–C as plastic-deformation-controlled, with wear-rate values described as roughly 7.0–7.6, and regions D–E as temperature-controlled, with values around 6.4–6.7. The article identifies aluminum material transfer on the HSS flank: in region A, a relatively smooth surface with parallel ridges showed Al transfer and adhesive pits. In region C, abrasive wear produced deeper plowing grooves and cracks, attributed to hard free-silicon particles in the die-cast alloy; particle size and silicon content influence wear. The excerpt does not provide a separate drill mass-loss measurement, a numerical wear-dimension value such as VB in micrometres, or a quantified amount of transferred aluminum or embedded abrasive particles. It also does not establish whether a built-up edge consists of aluminum versus tool metal; it only discusses built-up-edge removal and aluminum transfer.

## pqac-00000025

From text 'bhowmick2007neardrymachiningof pages 118-121'.

S Bhowmick. Near-dry machining of 319 aluminum-silicon alloy. Unknown journal, 2007.

The excerpt provides qualitative evidence of HSS drill degradation during repeated drilling, but it does not report a measured HSS flank-wear value, drill mass loss, tool-material transfer into the aluminium, or embedded abrasive-particle measurements. It attributes increasing torque, thrust, roughness, and subsurface damage to aluminium adhesion, built-up-edge (BUE) formation, chip clogging, and friction among the drill margin, chips, and hole wall. The drill is described as becoming dull because of aluminium adhesion. Type III drilling, associated with later holes and severe chip clogging, showed large amounts of transferred/adhered aluminium and surface deterioration. The BUE is specifically attributed to the soft aluminium matrix depositing on the cutting edges; the excerpt therefore supports an aluminium-based BUE rather than a BUE identified as HSS/tool metal. No quantitative BUE size, flank-wear dimension, or drill mass change is given. Quantified dimensions concern workpiece damage rather than tool wear: the fragmentation layer was approximately 15–20 μm thick, with broken second-phase particles measuring 2–6 μm, and the type III damaged subsurface zone reached approximately 80 μm. These values should not be interpreted as HSS flank-wear measurements.


---

## pqac-00000026

From text 'bhowmick2007neardrymachiningofa pages 118-121'.

S Bhowmick. Near-dry machining of 319 aluminum-silicon alloy. Unknown journal, 2007.

The excerpt concerns drilling 319 aluminum–silicon alloy with uncoated HSS drills and discusses aluminum adhesion, built-up edge (BUE), chip clogging, and resulting torque, surface roughness, and subsurface damage. It does not report a measured HSS flank-wear width, drill mass loss, wear-volume measurement, or direct transfer of HSS/tool material into the aluminum. The described adhered or transferred material is explicitly aluminum: the soft aluminum matrix deposits on the cutting edges and forms the BUE. Aluminum transfer was negligible in the type-I hole (second hole), limited initially but considerable later in type II (24th hole), and large in type III (47th hole), especially near chip clogging and the secondary torque peak. The excerpt attributes increased friction and torque to adhered aluminum between the drill, chips, and hole wall. Quantified dimensions relate to subsurface damage rather than tool wear: the type-II fragmentation layer was approximately 15–20 micrometers thick, with second-phase particles broken into 2–6 micrometer pieces, while type-III damage reached approximately 80 micrometers. No embedded abrasive-particle observations are reported in this passage.


---

## pqac-00000027

From text 'zhang2001wearmechanismmaps pages 1-2'.

M. Zhang, Yucheng Liu, and Hui Zhou. Wear mechanism maps of uncoated hss tools drilling die-cast aluminum alloy. Tribology International, 34:727-731, Nov 2001. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/s0301-679x(01)00058-5, doi:10.1016/s0301-679x(01)00058-5. This article has 43 citations and is from a domain leading peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt reports measured flank wear of uncoated W6Mo5Cr4V2 HSS drills during dry drilling of AlSi9Cu3 die-cast aluminum, but it does not provide individual numerical VB dimensions or the resulting wear-rate values in the supplied pages. Wear was measured as the flank-wear land length VB using a toolmaker’s microscope at 30× magnification with 100 µm accuracy, after drilling segments of 90 holes. Wear rate was normalized as log10(VB/cutting distance), and feed rate and cutting speed were used as the axes of the flank-wear map. The drills were treated with 5% NaOH to remove built-up edge before measurement, and SEM was used to examine worn surfaces. The excerpt identifies wear regimes including adhesive, adhesive–abrasive, abrasive, severe plastic flow, and thermal wear. However, these pages contain no measured drill mass loss, no quantified tool-material transfer into the aluminum, no quantified embedded abrasive particles, and no compositional determination of whether the built-up edge consisted of aluminum or tool metal. Although built-up edge removal is mentioned, its composition and dimensions are not reported in the supplied text.

## pqac-00000028

From text 'bhowmick2007neardrymachiningofa pages 139-142'.

S Bhowmick. Near-dry machining of 319 aluminum-silicon alloy. Unknown journal, 2007.

The excerpt reports drilling performance and aluminum transfer/adhesion, but it does not provide a measured HSS flank-wear dimension, drill mass loss, or evidence of embedded abrasive particles. For uncoated HSS drilling of 319 aluminum alloy, aluminum adhered to both the cutting edge and drill flutes; this adhesion eventually caused the drill to stick and defined failure at the 49th hole. The adhered aluminum mass after that hole was reported as 342 x 10'3 gm, and the maximum torque reached 7.96 N-m. The text also describes torque spikes as likely resulting from friction between adhered aluminum chips and the hole wall. H-DLC-coated drills showed much less material transfer: after 150 holes, adhered aluminum weighed 3.6 x 10'3 gm, and no drill failure occurred. NH-DLC drills likewise survived at least 150 holes, with 10.08 x 10'3 gm of adhered aluminum reported after 150 holes. Thus, the excerpt supports aluminum workpiece material transfer/build-up on the tool, rather than transfer of tool material into the aluminum. It does not identify a built-up-edge composition explicitly beyond describing adhered aluminum, and it contains no metallographic finding about tool-metal fragments or embedded abrasive particles.

Abstract:
Interfacial reactions drive all elemental cycling on Earth and play pivotal roles in human activities such as agriculture, water purification, energy production and storage, environmental contaminant remediation, and nuclear waste repository management. The onset of the 21st century marked the beginning of a more detailed understanding of mineral aqueous interfaces enabled by advances in techniques that use tunable high-flux focused ultrafast laser and X-ray sources to provide near-atomic measurement resolution, as well as by nanofabrication approaches that enable transmission electron microscopy in a liquid cell. This leap into atomic- and nanometer-scale measurements has uncovered scale-dependent phenomena whose reaction thermodynamics, kinetics, and pathways deviate from previous observations made on larger systems. A second key advance is new experimental evidence for what scientists hypothesized but could not test previously, namely, interfacial chemical reactions are frequently driven by "anomalies" or "non-idealities" such as defects, nanoconfinement, and other nontypical chemical structures. Third, progress in computational chemistry has yielded new insights that allow a move beyond simple schematics, leading to a molecular model of these complex interfaces. In combination with surface-sensitive measurements, we have gained knowledge of the interfacial structure and dynamics, including the underlying solid surface and the immediately adjacent water and aqueous ions, enabling a better definition of what constitutes the oxide- and silicate-water interfaces. This critical review discusses how science progresses from understanding ideal solid-water interfaces to more realistic systems, focusing on accomplishments in the last 20 years and identifying challenges and future opportunities for the community to address. We anticipate that the next 20 years will focus on understanding and predicting dynamic transient and reactive structures over greater spatial and temporal ranges as well as systems of greater structural and chemical complexity. Closer collaborations of theoretical and experimental experts across disciplines will continue to be critical to achieving this great aspiration.

Abstract:
We investigated the unique passive behaviour of Hybrid steel in de-aerated sulfuric acid and aqueous sodium chloride solutions through corrosion tests, surface analysis, and thermochemical modelling. Electrochemical measurements confirmed that Hybrid steel possesses stainless steel characteristics, including passivity, breakdown, and pitting, akin to low-alloyed stainless steel. Synchrotron hard X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy revealed a dynamically protective nanoscale passive film composed of Fe, Cr, Ni, and Al oxides, contributing to its stainless nature. The presence of Al and Ni enhances Cr’s role in forming a spontaneously passive and protective surface, resulting in exceptional corrosion resistance in acidic and chloride-containing solutions. Hybrid steel’s surface oxides remain robust even beyond the Cr(III)-to-Cr(VI) redox potential, distinguishing it from other stainless steels. This work demonstrates the potential for designing sustainable stainless steel with high-strength properties without requiring the conventional Cr threshold concentration of 10.5 per cent.

Abstract:
<jats:p>This review article summarizes the most widely used and effective technologies for producing protective and functional bilayer coatings. Particular attention is given to methods such as electroplating and electroless metallization, chemical vapor deposition, thermal spray and vacuum arc deposition, conversion treatments, laser modification, and organic layer deposition. Bilayer architectures are highlighted for their ability to overcome the limitations of single-layer coatings by combining complementary functionalities, resulting in enhanced adhesion, improved corrosion resistance through pore sealing or superhydrophobic surface states, and increased wear and crack resistance. This article is intended for researchers, materials scientists, and engineers engaged in surface engineering, corrosion protection, and advanced manufacturing, providing them with a clear understanding of the mechanisms, advantages, and practical applications of bilayer coatings. By synthesizing recent developments, comparative analyses, and performance data, the review enables readers to make informed decisions about the selection, design, and implementation of bilayer coatings for diverse industrial applications, ranging from aerospace and automotive components to medical devices and energy systems.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Liquid metal reaction media provides exciting new avenues for synthesizing low‐dimensional materials. Here, the synthesis of atomically thin sheets and nanofibers of boehmite (γ‐AlOOH) and their transformation into cubic alumina (γ‐Al2O3) via annealing is explored. The sheets are as thin as one orthorhombic boehmite unit cell. The addition of aluminum into a room temperature alloy of gallium, followed by exposing the melt to either liquid water or water vapor, allows growing either 2D sheets or 1D fibers, respectively. The isolated oxide hydroxides feature large surface areas, with the sheet morphologies also showing a high Young's modulus. The method is green, since the liquid metal solvent can be fully reused. The ultrathin boehmite sheets are found suitable for the development of freestanding membrane filters that enable excellent separation of heavy metal ions and oil from aqueous solutions at extraordinary filtrate flux. The developed liquid metal‐based synthesis process offers a sustainable, green, and rapid method for synthesizing nanomorphologies of metal oxides which are challenging to obtain by conventional methods. The process is both sustainable and scalable and may be explored for the creation of other types of metal oxide compounds.

Abstract:
Boehmite (γ-AlOOH) and gibbsite (α-Al-(OH)3) are important archetype (oxy)hydroxides of aluminum in nature that also play diverse roles across a plethora of industrial applications. Developing the ability to understand and predict the properties and characteristics of these materials, on the basis of their natural growth or synthesis pathways, is an important fundamental science enterprise with wide-ranging impacts. The present study describes bulk and surface characteristics of these novel materials in comprehensive detail, using a collectively sophisticated set of experimental capabilities, including a range of conventional laboratory solids analyses and national user facility analyses such as synchrotron X-ray absorption and scattering spectroscopies as well as small-angle neutron scattering. Their thermal stability is investigated using in situ temperature-dependent Raman spectroscopy. These pure and effectively defect-free materials are ideal for synthesis of advanced alumina products.

Abstract:
Drilling is one of the most performed machining operations for riveting and assembly operations in many industrial sectors. The accuracy of the drilled holes and their surface finish play a vital role in the longevity and performance of the machined components, which, in turn, increase productivity. Therefore, this study investigated the effect of the multi-spindle drilling process on dimensional hole tolerances, such as hole size, circularity, cylindricity, and perpendicularity. In addition, the surface defects formed in the holes were examined using scanning electron microscopy. Three aluminium alloys, AA2024, AA6061, and AA5083, which are commonly used in the aerospace, automotive, and marine sectors, were chosen as the study materials. The results showed that the holes drilled in AA2024 gave less circularity error, cylindricity error, and perpendicularity error. In the case of hole size, the holes drilled in AA6061 were less deviated from the nominal size following holes drilled in AA2024 and AA5083 alloys. Surface damage in the form of metal debris adhesion, smeared material, side flow, and feed marks was found on the inner hole surface. Holes drilled in AA5083 alloy had the worst surface finish and were the most oversized, which was associated with noticeable damage and deformations in their inner surface. The ANOVA results revealed that the spindle speed was more influential than feed and mainly affected the hole size and cylindricity errors. However, in the case of circularity error and perpendicularity error, drilling parameters were found to be insignificant.

Abstract:
Among the various types of metal matrix composites, SiC particle-reinforced aluminum matrix composites (SiCp/Al) are finding increasing applications in many industrial fields such as aerospace, automotive, and electronics. However, SiCp/Al composites are considered as difficult-to-cut materials due to the hard ceramic reinforcement, which causes severe machinability degradation by increasing cutting tool wear, cutting force, etc. To improve the machinability of SiCp/Al composites, many techniques including conventional and nonconventional machining processes have been employed. The purpose of this study is to evaluate the machining performance of SiCp/Al composites using conventional machining, i.e., turning, milling, drilling, and grinding, and using nonconventional machining, namely electrical discharge machining (EDM), powder mixed EDM, wire EDM, electrochemical machining, and newly developed high-efficiency machining technologies, e.g., blasting erosion arc machining. This research not only presents an overview of the machining aspects of SiCp/Al composites using various processing technologies but also establishes optimization parameters as reference of industry applications.

                    This paper presents a reformulation of the submarine alkaline hydrothermal theory for the emergence of life in response to recent experimental findings. In this case, the disequilibria were two: (1) in redox potential, between hydrogen
                    <jats:italic toggle="yes">plus</jats:italic>

The realization, now 50 years old, that membrane-spanning gradients, rather than organic intermediates, play a vital role in life's operations calls into question the idea of “prebiotic chemistry.” It informs our own suggestion that experimentation should look to the kind of nanoengines that must have been the precursors to molecular motors—such as pyrophosphate synthetase and the like driven by these gradients—that make life work. It is these putative free energy or disequilibria converters, presumably constructed from minerals comprising the earliest inorganic membranes, that, as obstacles to vectorial ionic flows, present themselves as
                    <jats:italic toggle="yes">the</jats:italic>
                    candidates for future experiments. Key Words: Methanotrophy—Origin of life. Astrobiology 14, 308–343.

Abstract:
Rotary degassing is one of the most frequently used melt treatment technologies used for processing liquid aluminum alloys. Despite this, the information available about the possible effects of this method on the double oxide- and nitride film (bifilm) content, especially when using different purging gases, is quite limited. For this reason, in this study, the effects of multiple rotary degassing treatments conducted with N2 and Ar purging gases on the bifilm quantity of a casting aluminum alloy were compared. The characterization of the melt quality was realized by the computed tomographic (CT) analysis of reduced pressure test (RPT) specimens, image analysis, and scanning electron microscopy (SEM) of the fracture surfaces of K-mold samples. Based on the results, by the application of Ar as a purging gas, relatively low bifilm content can be achieved. On the other hand, while the use of N2 leads to the formation of numerous small-sized nitride bifilms, which significantly increased the pore number density inside the RPT specimens. This can be associated with the nitride formation by the chemical reaction between the liquid aluminum alloy and the N2 purging gas bubbles during the degassing treatments.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Nickel–titanium (NiTi) shape memory alloys offer transformative functionality for biomedical and aerospace systems, yet their adoption in additive manufacturing (AM) remains constrained by powder reactivity, compositional sensitivity, and the high energy of feedstock production. This work establishes a unified, data-driven evaluation of how powder-state evolution during reuse and ultrasonic plasma atomization (UPA) affects both functional behavior and environmental performance. Virgin, reused, and UPA-recycled NiTi powders were systematically characterized based on particle-size distribution (PSD), SEM morphology, sphericity, oxygen content (ONH), and differential scanning calorimetry (DSC), and these results were coupled with a process-level life-cycle assessment (LCA) spanning cradle-to-gate feedstock generation. Reused powder showed finer but broadened PSD, surface oxidation, and elevated transformation temperatures; these degradation mechanisms limited its reuse despite reducing energy demand by ~30% relative to virgin powder. UPA provided a more effective regeneration pathway: UPA-recycled NiTi recovered high sphericity and smooth particle surfaces while lowering cradle-to-gate energy from 100 ± 10 to 50 ± 5 MJ·kg−1 (≈50%) and reducing CO2-equivalent emissions by ≈45%, with ~95% material recovery. Although the UPA condition exhibited a higher oxygen content in this study due to system-level atmosphere limitations, prior work indicates that optimized inert-gas control can suppress oxidation, suggesting clear avenues for improvement. Sustainability Index analysis confirmed UPA as the most favorable route, integrating reductions in energy demand and emissions with recovery of powder morphology and reconditioning of thermal transformation behavior. More broadly, the ability of UPA to promote compositional and microstructural redistribution highlights its potential to deliberately re-tune or “reprogram” transformation temperatures for application-specific requirements when alloying and processing atmospheres are carefully managed.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Gas-atomization is extensively used to produce metallic feedstock powders for additive manufacturing processes, including gas dynamic cold spray processing. This work explores the potential utility of on-demand recycled titanium scrap feedstock powder as a viable substitute for virgin powder sources. Three recycled titanium powders were atomized from different battlefield scrap sources using a mobile foundry developed by MolyWorks Materials Corporation. Recycled titanium alloy powders were compared against virgin Ti-6Al-4V powder to verify there were no significant variations between the recycled and virgin materials. Powder characterization methods included chemical analysis, particle size distribution analysis, scanning electron microscopy (SEM), Karl Fischer (KF) titration moisture content analysis, X-ray diffraction (XRD) phase analysis, microparticle compression testing (MCT), and nanoindentation. Results indicate that recycled titanium powder provides a viable alternative to virgin titanium alloy powders without compromising mechanical capabilities, microstructural features, or ASTM-specified composition and impurity standards. The results of this work will be used to aid future research efforts that will focus on optimizing cold spray parameters to maximize coating density, mechanical strength, and hardness of recycled titanium feedstock powders. “Cold spray” presents opportunities to enhance the sustainability of titanium component production through the utilization of recycled feedstock powder, mitigating issues of long lead times and high waste associated with the use of conventional virgin feedstock.

## pqac-00000029

From text 'lienhard2020surfaceoxideand pages 4-6'.

Jasper Lienhard, Cameron Crook, Maryam Zahiri Azar, Mostafa Hassani, Daniel R. Mumm, David Veysset, Diran Apelian, Keith A. Nelson, Victor Champagne, Aaron Nardi, Christopher A. Schuh, and Lorenzo Valdevit. Surface oxide and hydroxide effects on aluminum microparticle impact bonding. Acta Materialia, 197:28-39, Sep 2020. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.actamat.2020.07.011, doi:10.1016/j.actamat.2020.07.011. This article has 90 citations and is from a highest quality peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt quantifies aluminum powder passivation films using both XPS and TEM, with XPS representing an average over many particles and TEM sampling individual particles. As-received and thermally treated/dry baseline powders had smooth, uniform, fully amorphous films approximately 5–6 nm thick. Exposure to 50% relative humidity did not measurably increase film thickness, although surface roughening suggested incipient hydration. Exposure to 95% relative humidity produced a thicker film averaging approximately 8 nm, about a 45% relative increase over the control/dry condition, with larger thickness variations of roughly 3.5 nm and localized crystallinity. FTIR showed clear OH groups only for the RH-95 condition, consistent with hydration and formation of alumina oxyhydroxides. After heat treatment and vacuum desiccation (RH-95-D), the film became slightly thinner by less than 1 nm, more uniform, and showed no remaining crystallinity; the data indicate loss of hydroxide and partial recovery of a metastable oxide. The excerpt does not provide separate AlMg measurements, detailed thermal-desorption temperatures or OH quantities, nor data on machined 6xxx or 319 aluminum subsurface deformation, smeared material transfer, or coolant-corrosion staining.

## pqac-00000030

From text 'scottosheriff1999physicochemicalcharacterisationof pages 2-4'.

S. Scotto-Sheriff, E. Darque-Ceretti, G. Plassart, and M. Aucouturier. Physico-chemical characterisation of native air-formed oxide films on al-mg alloys at low temperature. influence of water. Journal of Materials Science, 34:5081-5088, Oct 1999. URL: https://doi.org/10.1023/a:1004709032754, doi:10.1023/a:1004709032754. This article has 37 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt provides XPS-based native oxide thicknesses for two Al-Mg alloys, but does not report machined 6xxx or 319 aluminum. The as-rolled A5182 alloy has an estimated oxide thickness of 4 nm, while annealed A5086 has an estimated thickness of 7 nm, indicating a 3 nm increase (approximately 75% thicker) after annealing. The oxide is chemically hydrated/hydroxylated rather than a purely dry Al2O3/MgO film. XPS O1s fitting identified Mg(OH)2 at 531.5 eV, combined Al2O3/MgO at 532.4 eV, AlO(OH) or Al(OH)3 at 533.5 eV, and H2O/contamination at 534.6 eV. The as-rolled sample showed four O1s components, whereas the annealed alloy showed three, with water apparently desorbed during annealing. Thermal dehydration was conducted at 300 °C for 3 hours under spectrometer-chamber vacuum; the high-binding-energy hydroxide contribution was nearly eliminated, confirming its association with aluminum hydroxides. The excerpt contains no quantitative measurements of machining-induced subsurface deformation, smeared material transfer, or coolant-corrosion staining.

Schuh, and Lorenzo Valdevit. Surface oxide and hydroxide effects on aluminum microparticle impact bonding. Acta Materialia, 197:28-39, Sep 2020. The excerpt provides XPS measurements for aluminum powder passivation films subjected to hot-air exposure. Across the as-received, HT-30, HT-60, and HT-240 conditions, the measured surface passivation layers remained approximately 5–6 nm thick, with reported XPS confidence intervals of about ±0.2–0.3 nm. Thus, within the tested hot-dry-air conditions, increasing heat-treatment duration did not produce a meaningful change in average XPS thickness. The article used FTIR over 800–4000 cm−1 and specifically considered the OH-stretching region near 2800–4000 cm−1, which is relevant to hydroxylated or hydrated surface species; however, the excerpt does not provide a quantitative dry-versus-water-hydrated thickness comparison or thermal-desorption OH values. It also does not quantify subsurface deformation, smeared material transfer, or coolant-corrosion staining for machined 6xxx or 319 aluminum. TEM and XPS generally agreed within approximately 1 nm, but the authors regarded XPS as more reliable for average thickness because it samples a much larger area. TEM was instead useful for assessing oxide crystallinity, uniformity, and roughness.

The excerpt characterizes native low-temperature air-formed oxide films on Al-Mg alloys, comparing as-rolled and annealed conditions. It reports that the oxide is thicker on the annealed alloy but remains below 10 nm; it does not provide a separate numerical XPS thickness for dry versus hydrated films. Both dry native films contain oxidized magnesium, metallic-state aluminum, and aluminum- and magnesium-containing hydroxides. The annealed film has a higher magnesium content and different magnesium distribution, attributed partly to crystallized alumina and enhanced Mg diffusion. After 90 seconds of hydration, the extreme surface becomes dominated by aluminum hydroxides: XPS O1s fitting shows reduced Mg(OH)2 and Al2O3/MgO contributions, while Al2p and Mg2p indicate lower relative Mg within the analyzed depth. Magnesium oxide and hydroxide are nearly totally dissolved from the as-rolled film but are mainly imbedded in the annealed film. Hydration produces pores and cracks, with protruding hydrated oxides and Al(OH)3 crystals reported for the annealed sample. The excerpt contains no thermal-desorption OH quantification, no direct dry/hydrated thickness values derived from XPS, and no data on machined 6xxx or 319 aluminum, subsurface deformation, smeared transfer, coolant corrosion, or staining.

## pqac-00000033

From text 'czech2010hydrogengenerationfrom pages 72-77'.

Edith Barbara Czech. Hydrogen generation from aluminum-water systems. ArXiv, Jan 2010. URL: https://doi.org/10.14288/1.0078738, doi:10.14288/1.0078738. This article has 4 citations.

The excerpt provides XPS-based estimates for native/surface oxide-film thickness on aluminum powders, but not specifically Al-Mg alloys or machined 6xxx/319 material. The as-received Al powder has an estimated oxide thickness of 3.2–9.6 nm, while water-washed (“washed-out”) Al has a thicker 4.6–13.8 nm film. Freshly ball-milled Al-NaCl powder has the thinnest listed film, 1.6–4.8 nm. The corresponding oxide-to-metal atomic intensity ratios are 3.88:1, 8.88:1, and 1.15:1, respectively. XPS O 1s spectra are broad and centered near 532.25 eV; hydroxide/hydroxyl oxygen is identified as the predominant near-surface species, with possible overlap from oxide and chemisorbed water.      4. Conclusion
  A preliminary comparison between powders derived from secondary alloy or scrap feedstock for two aluminium alloys belonging to
    the aluminium-silicon (4.xxx) and aluminium-copper (2.xxx) categories is presented within the context of this study.
   The study demonstrates that aluminium powders derived from both ingots and industrial scrap exhibit comparable quality, with
    minor variations in light element content due to potential contamination from process fluids in scrap alloys.
   The SEM analysis revealed that both types of powders are highly spherical, as confirmed by quantitative image analysis. The high
    convexity of powders can be considered a relevant indicator of an extremely low satellite content.
    Different methods for measuring flowability showed comparable trends, for both the EN AC 46000 and AA 2024 powders.
    Significant differences were observed only for the AA 2024 powders, with reduced flowability for the scrap alloy powders compared
    to the ingot powders. Further investigations are underway to characterise the surface state from a chemical point of view to correlate
    with flow properties. The validation and subsequent adoption of powders obtained from scrap feedstock would promote sustainable
    practices in manufacturing towards a reduction in CO2 emissions.

   The atomized alloys were sieved below 250µm to separate the atomization debris eventually formed, and the collected powder was
    sieved in the 20-63 µm range suitable for L-PBF; the characterizations proposed were performed in that powder size interval. The
   powder microstructure and morphology was observed by scanning electron microscopy from the top, after mounting a small sample
    of powders on a carbon tape disc.

    2.3.1 Light elements concentration (O, N, H, C and S)
   The quantities of oxygen, nitrogen and hydrogen were assessed in the atomized powders using the elemental analyzer (LECO
   ONH836). This analysis provided insights into the oxygen, hydrogen and nitrogen contents at various particle sizes, revealing
    possible variations between ingot and scrap powders.
    Further analyses were performed to assess the quality of the powders in terms of carbon and sulfur content (LECO CS744).

    2.3.2 Powder rheology
   The rheological properties of the powders were characterized using a shear cell rheometer (Freeman Technology FT4). The
    rheological properties of the powders at constant shear rate and their stability were quantified by measuring the specific energy (SE),
     stability index (SI) and basic flow energy (BFE). The influence of shear rate on powder flowability was quantified by the Flow Rate
    Index (FRI). Shear cell rheology data were compared with conventional Hall funnel flowability (according to ASTM B213). Powder
    sampling for this test was based on alloy density and therefore comparisons are only consistent between powders of the same
    chemical composition (e.g. AA 2024 new vs. AA 2024 scrap). All powders were dried under vacuum at 80°C to reduce the moisture
    content.

    2.3.4 Powder morphology
  A quantitative assessment of powder morphology was performed by optical image analysis (Malvern Morphology). More than 2*104
     particles was analyzed per each batch produced and the average values of circularity, convexity and aspect ratio are presented.

    detected in the scrap alloy is supposed to be related to the scrap cleanliness due to possible contamination by process fluids

    Considering the powders obtained from the modified AA 2024 alloy, a higher amount of oxygen was detected for the scrap powders.
     Interestingly, compared to the 4.xxx series alloy, a slight increase in the nitrogen content was observed and remarkable increase in

    Abstract
     Inert gas atomization is a suitable technique for producing highly spherical powders used in metal additive manufacturing and other
   powder metallurgy techniques. Research into environmental sustainability is leading to new considerations in metal powder quality,
    gas atomisation processes, and raw material selection. This work presents the properties and sustainability of some gas-atomised
    aluminium-based powders. This study compares the characteristics of  final powders made from conventional or innovative
    aluminum-based alloys belonging to the 2.xxx and 4.xxx series, using secondary or scrap materials. The comparison is based on
    granulometry, morphology, microstructure, and chemical composition, including light elements such as O, N, H, C, and S.

   Keywords: gas atomization, sustainability, aluminum alloys.

     1. Introduction
    Sustainability and environmental concerns are critical in industrial practices, making the assessment of the environmental impact of
    materials and manufacturing processes increasingly studied. Aluminium, renowned for  its excellent strength-to-weight  ratio,
    corrosion resistance, and versatility, is a key material across various industries, including transportation and construction. As the push
    for sustainable practices intensifies, the recycling of aluminium alloys has become more significant. Currently, 37% of Europe's
    aluminium production involves recycled alloys, and this percentage is expected to grow due to the substantial energy savings—up to
   95%—achieved through re-melting compared to primary production 1-4.

    In the automotive sector, aluminium alloys belonging to the 4.xxx series such as AlSi10Mg and AlSi9Cu3(Fe) are extensively used
    in high-pressure  die casting (HPDC) because of  their superior mechanical  properties and  castability. However,  traditional
    manufacturing processes produce a considerable amount of scrap, leading to resource wastage and environmental issues. Despite
     efforts to minimize defective castings, some scrap is unavoidable and must be either recycled or repurposed.
      It is important to differentiate between new scraps, which are generated during production, and old scraps, which are end-of-life
    components and often contaminated with iron. Scrap alloys from foundry which have a high iron content, tend to produce more slag.
    Studies indicate that re-melting these alloys can alter their chemical composition and mechanical properties, although this process
    can still yield good results with proper management 5-6.

    Although research on AlSi9Cu3(Fe) for AM is limited, initial findings are promising. Comparisons with AlSi10Mg powders indicate
    potential for high performance in AM applications. Thorough characterization of key powder properties, such as density, particle size
     distribution, and rheology, is necessary to ensure quality and processability.
    Repurposing production scraps for additive manufacturing (AM) presents a sustainable and economically feasible approach. These
    scrap materials can be converted into high-quality powders through gas atomization, suitable for Laser Powder Bed Fusion (L-PBF)
    processes, and can produce automotive components with excellent tensile properties 6-9.

   Among the emerging literature regarding sustainability and metallurgy, a comprehensive point of view is presented in the review by
   Raabe 10. The concepts of dirty alloys is addressed as the most effective way to reduce the massive CO2 emission footprint of
    metallic materials by producing them through secondary synthesis, i.e. from scrap. In the aerospace, 2.xxx series aluminium alloys,
     like Al-Cu alloys, are extensively employed due to their superior mechanical properties and high fatigue resistance. However,
     traditional manufacturing processes generate substantial scrap, resulting in resource wastage and environmental challenges. Despite
     efforts to reduce defective parts, some scrap generation is inevitable due to the mechanical working required to produce the final
    parts and requires either recycling or repurposing.

   Due to the low amount of scrap produced during part manufacturing, AM technologies are considered a sustainable and lean
    manufacturing processes, nevertheless the properties of the starting powders represent a crucial aspect for processability. Within the
    frame of the work, the results from the production and the characterization of gas atomized powders are presented comparing the
    properties of powders obtained from ingots or scrap feedstocks.

Abstract:

 
 Additive manufacturing of metal materials is one of the most promising technologies in modern industry. A wide variety of current additive manufacturing techniques allow rapid prototyping and industrial production of different-sized products from various structural and functional materials. The structure and physical-mechanical properties of the metal products fabricated by electron-beam additive manufacturing (EBAM) within nonstationary metallurgy in a local molten pool often differ from those of the products fabricated by conventional metallurgy due to different crystallization mechanisms, sequence and completeness of phase transformations, and heterogeneous/homogeneous chemical composition of the resulting material. The possibility to control local metallurgical processes in the molten pool is the key advantage of the EBAM technology. It allows one to control the structure, composition, and properties of mono- and polymetallic, graded, composite and heat-resistant materials in order to obtain products with the desired chemical composition, macroscopic architecture, and microscopic structural parameters. As any new industrial technology, the EBAM method requires the development of scientifically based approaches to the choice of materials and production conditions. Here we provide an overview of the scientific approaches developed for electron-beam additive manufacturing of products from metals and alloys using wire or rods as a feedstock. The range of the studied materials includes additive materials based on copper, bronze, aluminum, nickel, titanium alloys, and different steels, as well as aluminum-based functionally graded materials and copper-based graded materials. The most important research findings are summarized.

Abstract:
Abstract
Laser welding of advanced Al-Li alloys has been developed to meet the increasing demand for light-weight and high-strength aerospace structures. However, welding of high-strength Al-Li alloys can be problematic due to the tendency for hot cracking. Finding suitable welding parameters and filler material for this combination currently requires extensive and costly trial and error experimentation. The present work describes a novel coupled model to predict hot crack susceptibility (HCS) in Al-Li welds. Such a model can be used to shortcut the weld development process. The coupled model combines finite element process simulation with a two-level HCS model. The finite element process model predicts thermal field data for the subsequent HCS hot cracking prediction. The model can be used to predict the influences of filler wire composition and welding parameters on HCS. The modeling results have been validated by comparing predictions with results from fully instrumented laser welds performed under a range of process parameters and analyzed using high-resolution X-ray tomography to identify weld defects. It is shown that the model is capable of accurately predicting the thermal field around the weld and the trend of HCS as a function of process parameters.

Abstract:
The advancement of friction stir welding for joining of aluminum alloys and aluminum centered matrix composite has replaced the traditional welding techniques. In this experimental study, AA6063/10.5wt%SiC composite has been produced by employing enhanced stir casting technique with the assistance of Mg metal powder. Specimen composite plates having thickness 6 mm were friction stir welded successfully. The impact of welding variables on mechanical and microstructural characteristics of weldments has been studied. The friction stir welding (FSW) was carried out at a rotation rate of tool of 1400 rpm with a tool transverse rate of 124 mm/min. A cylindrical tool fabricated of high-speed steel (HSS) with square pin shape has been used for FSW. The results revealed that the ultimate tensile strength of the welded joint was 163 MPa, which was very close to the strength of the as-cast composite matrix. The microstructural study showed the reason for higher joint strength and microhardness. The welded butt joint exhibited a change in the microstructure at various four welding zones which transforms the mechanical characteristics of welded joints has been due to the asymmetrical flow of material and thermal cycles around the pin. The intense stirring action of the tool pin during FSW cracked the SiC particles in the weld nugget.  In the weld region, a fine-grained structure and homogeneous dispersion of SiC particles have been observed. The micro porosities associated with the base metal composite matrix were eliminated after FSW.

## 2. A Metallurgically Informed Multiscale Integrated Computational Framework for Metal Forming Processes

Abstract:
: Predicting the mechanical response of industrial alloys is crucial for optimizing manufacturing processes and improving material performance. Traditional, solely experimental approaches, though effective, are inefficient as they are resource-intensive, requiring extensive laboratory testing and the iterative calibration of processing conditions. These costs can be avoided through computational/virtual experiments based on a multiscale hierarchical framework that integrates macroscopic approaches, mesoscale modelling as well as atomic level and advanced thermodynamical simulations to study and predict the mechanical response of metallic systems. In the context of this work, a framework for studying the effect of forming on metallic materials is proposed, applied, and validated on the hot extrusion of AA6063. Coupling thermodynamic simulations (including Phase Field) results with literature data establishes a microstructurally accurate representative volume element (RVE) design. This way, the phase fraction and the grain size of the RVE are determined by thermodynamic simulations (ThermoCalc, MICRESS), which can be validated via microstructure characterization. It is known that the mechanical properties of the individual phases affect the macroscopical properties of the material. Using atomic level simulations (i.e., molecular dynamics), the dislocation density of the material is calculated and utilized as an input for a Crystal Plasticity Fast Fourier Transformation simulation. This iterative process can be applied to match all stages of manufacturing processes. The hierarchical and systematic integration of these computational methodologies enables a rigorous analysis of the effect that processing parameters have on the microstructure. This work contributes to the broader effort of creating experiment-free workflows for designing materials and processes by leveraging a multiscale modeling approach. Coupled with experimental data, the predictive accuracy of the mechanical behavior can be further enhanced.

Abstract:
Friction surfacing is one of the recent technologies applied in surface engineering for the development of surface materials. It is a solid-state technique employed to coat one material over the another in order to reconstruct the worn-out parts. Friction surfacing is done to enhance the wear and corrosion resistance, as well as mechanical properties in materials. It is an environmentally safe process in which a consumable rod is deformed plastically and forms a deposit of viscoelastic material over the substrate. In this study, aluminum alloys (AA), such as, AA6061 and AA6063 were deposited over mild steel by friction surfacing process. The consumable aluminium alloys were provided a constant rotational speed of 2000 rpm and axial force of 10 kN, at three different travel speeds of 250 mm/min, 400 mm/min and 630 mm/min for the deposition of aluminium over mild steel substrate plate. The AA-samples were prepared by “wire electric discharge machining (WEDM)” process and were finished by rotating wheel polishing machine. The thickness and width of the coatings were measured after the deposition. The ‘optical microscope’ and ‘field emission scanning electron microscope (FESEM)’ were utilized to do the microstructural assessment of the deposited surface. The surface roughness was analyzed by non-contact type profilometer. The X-ray diffraction (XRD) and energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) analysis were performed for the study of different phases present in the coating samples. The hardness variation over the coating surface due to varying travel speed was measured by Vickers micro hardness tester. The coating done by AA6063 alloy was found harder than the coating of AA6061. The surface roughness of aluminum alloy AA6063 coating is higher at 250 mm/min and slightly less at 630 mm/min, compared to aluminum alloy AA6061 coating. In addition, examination of the interface area of aluminium deposit over mild steel was done using FESEM. Through EDS elemental analysis it is established that aluminium is present in more than 90% with other elements like Mg and Si. By XRD analysis high intensity peaks of aluminium were recorded on different planes. Results show poor bonding between layers at 250 mm/min and 630 mm/min, while good bonding at 400 mm/min which improves properties.

Abstract:
<jats:p>This study aims to refine a rheo-stir casting method for producing aluminium alloy 6063-based metal matrix composite reinforced with tungsten carbide at varying concentrations ranging from 0.2% to 1% by weight. AA6063/0.6WC composite was subjected to additional testing, and this shows how operations, including solution heat treatment and rolling under different circumstances, impacted the material. A closer look at the microstructure reveals that the pining effect caused by the integration of WC into the AA6063 matrix resulted in grain refinement. As the amount of increasing WC addition, the material’s mechanical characteristics enhanced. The composite with 1 wt.% WC exhibited the maximum microhardness (98 Hv), Ultimate tensile strength (UTS) (235 MPa) and Yield strength (YS) (210 MPa) due to the dispersion strengthening mechanism. The densification and particle dispersion of AA6063/WC composites were greatly improved by the rheo stir casting method. Hardness was improved by precipitation hardening after the secondary phases were dissolved in a homogenization procedure. Because dynamic recovery was inhibited during cryo-rolling, the resulting specimen had the maximum hardness of 178 Hv among all rolling techniques while being 80% thinner. It was shown that experimental YS was greater than theoretical YS after accounting for the impact of the strengthening processes.</jats:p>

Andrey Filippov, Veronika Utyaganova, Nikolay Shamarin, Andrey Vorontsov, Nikolay Savchenko, Denis Gurianov, Andrey Chumaevskii, Valery Rubtsov, Evgeny Kolubaev, and Sergei Tarasov. Microstructure and corrosion resistance of aa4047/aa7075 transition zone formed using electron beam wire-feed additive manufacturing. Materials, 14:6931, Nov 2021. URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/ma14226931, doi:10.3390/ma14226931. This article has 18 citations.

The excerpt is only partially relevant to the requested comparison of published AA6063 and AA4047 composition limits. It does not state the formal AA6063 upper limits (Fe 0.35, Cu 0.10, Mg 0.45–0.9, Si 0.2–0.6, Cr 0.10, Mn 0.10) or the formal AA4047 limits (Fe ≤0.8, Cu ≤0.3, Si 11–13). It also does not provide a standards-based distinction between nominal/formal alloy limits and measured product composition. Instead, the paper reports local, experimentally measured composition and phases in an AA4047/AA7075 additively manufactured wall and transition zone. EDS profiles show Mg, Zn, and Cu decreasing sharply through the transition zone while Si increases. The deposited AA4047 region contains α-Al and Al/Si eutectic structures, with some Fe-Si-Al-related phases. The transition zone contains intermixed alloy material and locally measured Mg levels up to 2.5 at.%, while XRD identifies α-Al, Si, and MgZn2. These values describe the particular deposited material and spatially varying microstructure; they should not be treated as certification of AA4047 composition limits or as a substitute for a published chemical-composition specification.

                       Traditional metal forming relies on empirical models that lack predictive accuracy
                             across length scales. Recent advances in ICME enable multiscale modeling, but challenges
                         remain in coupling metallurgical insights with computational models, especially across
                            length scales.
                              There are papers focused on multiscale simulations in order to bridge the effect of
                         manufacturing on the microstructure with its impact on the final properties. There are
                           various models and combinations for each manufacturing stage that can yield satisfac-
                            tory results [9], with each having unique strengths and weaknesses. An approach that

                        modeling to capture thermal gradients during manufacturing, a phase field model that

                                crystal plasticity model that captures the mechanical response of the system in the additive
                         manufacturing of titanium alloys is presented in [10]. In another example from additive
                          manufacturing [11], the coupled models were CalPhaD, FEM, Kinetic Monte Carlo, DFT,
                       and physics-based CP were utilized in a similar manner.
                                This work develops a hierarchical, iterative, and physics-based multiscale framework
                              to address these challenges, integrating phase field modeling, molecular dynamics, and
                                crystal plasticity simulations. The framework introduced for studying the effect of forming
                        on metallic materials is applied and validated on the hot extrusion of AA6063. The CalPhaD
                          method, in combination with KWN, can be used to quantify the microstructural constituents
                                 after each step, whereas the PF can be used to study the grain size after each thermal cycle.
                        The physics-based CP allows for integration with lower scale models, such as MD. ThroughCrystals 2025, 15, 399                                                                                                           3 of 15

info.name: collect_cited_papers_in_evidence
info.description:
Collect papers by traversing the citations of relevant papers to increase the paper count.

This tool has no effect if called when paper count or relevant papers are zero.
This tool will find papers that are likely to lead to more relevant evidence.
The papers found have a higher chance of relevance because this tool starts from relevant evidence.
This tool's usefulness increases with the amount of gathered evidence as there's more citations to consider.

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

info.name: patent_search
info.description:
Search for patents to increase the patent count.

Repeat previous calls with the same query to continue a search.
Only repeat a maximum of three times.
This tool can be called concurrently.
This tool introduces novel patents, so invoke it when just beginning
or when unsatisfied with the current evidence.

query.description:
A search query for patents (using Google Patents). Never include temporal
filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)

Minimum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

question.description: Specific question to gather evidence for.
question.title: Question

text_name_focus_list.description:
if there are known text names that are relevant to the question,
you can specify them here. This will ensure that the tool will look at these text names
first, and then look at the rest of the evidence. If left as `None`, an embedding
search will be performed on underlying content to find most relevant texts.
text_name_focus_list.title: Text Name Focus List
