{"answer": "# Machining contamination of 6063 cups for Al–Si atomization

**Bottom line.** Published measurements show that an apparently wiped aluminum surface can retain oil at tens to roughly 150 mg/m², but they do **not** establish the residual loading after the particular IPA/Kimwipe procedure described here. For a cup having 60 cm² of exposed surface, 1 mg/m² corresponds to 6 µg per cup, or 0.12 ppm by mass in a 50 g cup. Oil is likely to outgas or decompose rather than enter the powder quantitatively; oxide, entrained solids, and some carbon- or hydrogen-bearing reaction products are more credible surviving hazards. There is no defensible published *per-cup* survival fraction for this process. (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000013, pqac-00000046)

## (a) Cutting-fluid films and wiping

An FTIR study provides **analogues, not measurements on drilled 6063**. Applying oil to aluminum foil and thoroughly wiping off the excess with *dry tissue* left approximately **150 mg/m²** (15 µg/cm²). An aluminum rod contaminated with silicone lubricant gave **49–77 mg/m²** by two spectral bands; a mineral-oil stain on sandblasted 7075 corresponded to approximately **280 mg/m²**. The same investigators reported detection of hydrocarbon films around **1 mg/m²** under favorable conditions. None of those values is an IPA-wipe endpoint or a representative distribution for an uncontrolled shop lathe. (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000004, pqac-00000005, pqac-00000008)

| Surface loading, illustrative | µg/cm² | Residue on 60 cm² cup | If divided by 50 g cup | If four cups supply 200 g melt |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 mg/m², approximately the favorable FTIR detection level | 0.10 | 6 µg | 0.12 ppm | 0.12 ppm |
| 49–77 mg/m², silicone on an aluminum rod | 4.9–7.7 | 0.294–0.462 mg | 5.9–9.2 ppm | 5.9–9.2 ppm |
| 150 mg/m², oil after *dry-tissue* wiping of foil | 15 | 0.90 mg | 18 ppm | 18 ppm |
| 280 mg/m², deliberate mineral-oil stain on 7075 | 28 | 1.68 mg | 34 ppm | 34 ppm |

The arithmetic is **total surface residue divided by metal mass**, not measured dissolved carbon, hydrogen, or final-powder concentration. For the actual charge, use the **measured** masses of the cups, plugs, and contained powder: the stated 50 g per cup and approximately 200 g per four-cup run are approximate. An estimated film thickness can also be misleading inside a blind, rough bore: pooled coolant or trapped chips need not resemble a uniform film. (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000004, pqac-00000008)

**After IPA/Kimwipes:** no study retrieved measured µg/cm² remaining after that procedure on an equivalently deep aluminum bore. IPA may remove accessible, soluble oil, but wiping does not certify removal of recessed pools, dried water-soluble-coolant additives, adherent inorganic particles, or native oxide. As a useful *contrast*, optimized **distillation of 7075 chips removed 99.7% of oil and water**; that result cannot be assigned to a brief IPA wipe. Neither “zero residue” nor a particular cleaning percentage is supported for these cups. (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000005, pqac-00000006)

## (b) Tool metal, built-up edge, and shop particles

A dry-drilling study on **harder, Si-rich die-cast AlSi9Cu3**, using W6Mo5Cr4V2 HSS drills, documented adhesive, abrasive, and severe thermal wear. It measured drill-flank wear after batches of **90 holes**, but reported a normalized wear map—not a reliable drill **mass loss per hole** or Fe/W/Mo/Cr/V transferred into each workpiece. Its numerical wear-map indices must not be interpreted as milligrams of HSS in a cup. The observed material adhering to the drill was **aluminum from the workpiece**. In another Al–Si drilling study, adhered aluminum on an uncoated HSS drill reached a reported **342 mg after 49 holes**; this is aluminum *on the tool*, emphatically **not** HSS deposited in 49 parts. Neither test predicts a mass-loss rate for drilling soft 6063 with a 12.7 mm drill. (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000010, pqac-00000022, pqac-00000025)

WC–Co wear could introduce W and Co if a carbide turning tool chips or wears, whereas the specified HSS bore drill principally poses Fe and its actual grade-specific alloying elements; **Co is not universal to HSS**. Steel/brass swarf or particles from shared equipment can add Fe, Cu, and Zn. Aluminum-hole studies directly describe smeared metal and adhering debris; however, no applicable study retrieved quantifies WC–Co transfer, entrapped steel/brass swarf, or SiC/Al₂O₃ grit per cleaned 6063 cup. These are plausible *discrete-particle* risks, especially after filing or emery use, not justified ppm estimates. A single **1 mg** particle retained in **200 g** of charge would represent **5 ppm of that particle’s mass** if fully incorporated; its constituent-element ppm would depend on its composition and retention. Because a particle may remain as an inclusion, even a low bulk ppm need not establish LPBF acceptability. (pqac-00000023, pqac-00000024, pqac-00000037)

## (c) Altered aluminum surface

Fresh aluminum rapidly passivates; an often-reported room-temperature air-film range is **2–5 nm**. Specific Al–Mg alloy surfaces measured by XPS carried approximately **4 nm** and **7 nm** films. These are analogues, not a measured oxide thickness on this machined 6063. Water can change *chemistry as well as thickness*: aluminum micropowder film thickness was approximately **5–6 nm** in a dry/control condition and approximately **8 nm** after exposure to **95% relative humidity**, with hydroxide/OH evidence; 50% humidity did not measurably increase its thickness. Brief hydration of Al–Mg surfaces also changed their outer layer toward hydroxides. IPA wiping cannot undo that oxide. (pqac-00000029, pqac-00000030, pqac-00000032, pqac-00000036)

A water-based coolant therefore adds a credible route to hydrated oxide, retained salts/additives, and localized staining **if it remains wet or dries on the metal**; it does not imply that every coolant-treated cup acquires an 8 nm film or significant corrosion. A finishing investigation describes aluminum’s approximate passive **pH 4–9** range, chloride-associated pitting, effects of copper-containing rinse water, and halo-like corrosion where coolant dries. Separately, drilling **319 Al–Si** produced a **15–20 µm** near-surface fragmentation layer in one condition and damage extending to **80 µm** with severe chip clogging. These are workpiece damage depths in a different alloy and cutting regime, **not** a measured cold-worked depth or new chemical contaminant inventory in 6063; cold work itself loses its deformed microstructure on complete melting. (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000037, pqac-00000038)

A simple scale calculation puts the oxide in perspective: taking **60 cm²**, a *uniform* **2–5 nm Al₂O₃** layer, density approximately **3.9 g/cm³**, and Al₂O₃ oxygen mass fraction **0.471** gives approximately **22–55 µg oxygen per cup**. If all four films’ oxygen entered a **200 g** melt, the *maximum mass-balance contribution under these assumptions* would be approximately **0.44–1.1 ppm O**. Roughness, patchy/hydrated films, other exposed surfaces, oxide removal into dross, and the powder already inside the cups invalidate this as a measured melt-O increment. The calculation underscores why a small **particle or retained coolant deposit**, rather than a pristine native film, may dominate contamination from machining. (pqac-00000030, pqac-00000036)

## (d) What remelting can—and cannot—remove

Pump-down favors removal of **volatile** IPA, water, and lighter hydrocarbons *provided they can escape before the sealed or tightly packed charge melts*. The small **1 mm vent** and a powder-filled, blind cavity make this a process-dependent condition, not evidence of complete degassing. Nonvolatile lubricant additives, salts, and grit will not evaporate merely because the chamber was pumped down. Upon heating, residual organics can volatilize or decompose; water and hydrated surface species can supply hydrogen through reactions with aluminum. Insoluble oxides may collect in surface dross or be entrained as films/particles; an argon backfill is not a chemical deoxidizer. Aluminum-chip recycling literature explicitly requires cutting-fluid removal and warns about gases during uncleaned remelting, but gives no IPA-wipe-to-powder survival percentage. (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000001, pqac-00000043, pqac-00000046)

There is **direct but non-identical feedstock-to-powder evidence**. In one vacuum-induction/argon **gas-atomization** comparison, 20–63 µm powder from Al–Si casting-alloy scrap contained **0.023 ± 0.006 wt% C**, versus **0.013 ± 0.003 wt% C** from ingot; oxygen was **0.036 ± 0.010** versus **0.049 ± 0.016 wt%**, respectively, and H was approximately **5 ppm in both**. For a *different*, modified AA2024 alloy, scrap/ingot powders contained **0.021 ± 0.005/0.011 ± 0.001 wt% C**, **0.068 ± 0.013/0.048 ± 0.013 wt% O**, and **53 ± 13/17 ± 3 ppm H**. Authors suspected scrap process fluids as one cause of elevated carbon, while noting some contamination entered slag. Starting scrap and ingot compositions differed; these are **associations, not a controlled oil-dose experiment**, and the atomizer was not this BN-washed graphite/40 kHz ultrasonic apparatus. They show why neither “vacuum removes everything” nor “all surface oil becomes carbon in powder” follows from evidence. (pqac-00000046, pqac-00000047, pqac-00000048)

Likewise, oxygen is not interchangeable with hydrogen or carbon: some oxide is separated, some can remain entrained, and fresh droplets subsequently oxidize on exposure. Hydrogen is a porosity concern because its solubility falls on solidification, while oxide films/inclusions can act as defect sites. A moisture-exposure/remelting investigation measured hydrogen increases for its specific aluminum specimens, including **0.04 ppm H** on heating commercially pure Al in air and **0.279 ppm H** for Mg-containing 5083 in air; these values are **not** predicted pickup in the present charge. Powder-processing studies provide a closer LPBF warning: AlSi10Mg reused for more than 30 months rose from roughly **0.05 to 0.12 wt% O** and **80 to 130 ppm H**, with part porosity changing from **<1% to approximately 3%** under virgin-powder-qualified parameters. In a separate, deliberately severe **400 °C/96 h air-aging** test, powder oxygen rose from **0.072 to 0.274 wt%** and manufactured-part porosity from **3.52 to 6.50%**; oxygen aging, changed laser absorption, and process behavior confound a simple causal attribution to oxygen alone. These are **powder aging/reuse**, not tests of dirty cups. (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000016, pqac-00000017, pqac-00000020, pqac-00000039, pqac-00000059)

**Carbon/carbide qualification:** a graphite/Si–Al melt study found graphite attack and carbide formation at **1500 °C** under vacuum, not at **800–840 °C** in a BN-washed crucible. It does not establish an Al₄C₃ production rate here, nor prove that residual WD-40 or cutting oil converts quantitatively to Al₄C₃. A BN wash may reduce direct graphite contact, but its actual coverage and integrity matter. Abrasive **Al₂O₃** should be treated as a possible refractory inclusion; **SiC** can remain particulate or react depending on melt contact and residence time. No retrieved measurement establishes the amount surviving this particular nozzle/sonotrode route. (pqac-00000041)

## (e) Alloy chemistry versus powder oxygen

A published table of generally used **AA6063 compositional limits** gives **Si 0.20–0.60 wt%, Mg 0.45–0.90 wt%, Fe <0.35 wt%, Cu <0.10 wt%, Mn <0.10 wt%, and Cr <0.10 wt%**. Published AA4047 work identifies its characteristic **11–13 wt% Si**; one actual AA4047 wire contained **11.85% Si, 0.199% Fe, and 0.006% Cu**. Those **wire analyses are not AA4047 impurity limits**: the exact 4047 Fe/Cu maximum applicable to the purchased AA4047 powder should be checked against its certificate and governing specification rather than inferred from that wire. Nor do 6063 *limits* reveal the composition of the particular 6063 bar. (pqac-00000054, pqac-00000061, pqac-00000063)

**Most importantly, the cups are part of the charge, not just contaminated containers.** Using the question’s approximate masses, **200 g of 6063 cups/plugs** and **36–56 g of 4047 powder** would produce approximately **78–85 wt% 6063** before accounting for any other metal. Its nominal Si concentration would then be only approximately **1.9–3.5 wt%** if the 6063 contains 0.20–0.60% Si and the 4047 contains 11–13% Si—not Al–12Si. The range combines endpoints and is an arithmetic illustration, not a melt analysis. Even at the 6063 Fe ceiling, cups could contribute up to approximately **0.27–0.30 wt% Fe to the combined charge**; at its Cu ceiling, up to approximately **0.078–0.085 wt% Cu**, *before* contributions from 4047 or foreign swarf. By contrast, **1 mg** of fully incorporated pure Fe in a **200 g** run is **5 ppm Fe = 0.0005 wt%**. Bulk alloy mixing can therefore outweigh ordinary trace tool wear, while a localized steel/brass or abrasive inclusion remains a separate defect issue. If “~200 g total” instead denotes *all* metal including the 4047, reweighing each input is essential before applying those illustrative fractions. (pqac-00000054, pqac-00000061, pqac-00000063)

Finally, the powder’s **own surface area** is much larger than the cups’. A spherical-particle calculation for 200 g of aluminum-density material, density approximately **2.7 g/cm³** and diameter **15–45 µm**, gives approximately **10–30 m²** of powder surface, against approximately **0.024 m²** for four nominal 60 cm² cups. With a hypothetical uniform **3–5 nm Al₂O₃** shell, oxygen would be approximately **0.06–0.30 wt%** across those diameter/thickness endpoints; *not* a measured value for this Al–Si lot. Direct hot-gas-extraction data provide the better benchmark: fresh AlSi10Mg was **0.067 wt% O** in one study and approximately **0.05 wt% O** in another, whereas gas-atomized Al–Si casting-alloy powder was **0.036–0.049 wt% O** in the scrap/ingot comparison. These are **hundreds of ppm oxygen in powder**, versus the approximately **0.4–1.1 ppm O upper-bound arithmetic** for four idealized pristine cup oxides. The cup calculation must not be read as an upper bound for coolant corrosion, inclusions, air exposure during atomization, or the original **36–56 g** of 4047 powder; obtain an actual O/N/H/C analysis of both incoming and produced size fractions for this system. (pqac-00000014, pqac-00000017, pqac-00000044, pqac-00000046)

**Evidence limit:** No located publication measures the combined sequence—uncontrolled manual turning/deep HSS drilling of 6063, the stated IPA/Kimwipe wipe, BN-washed graphite melting at 800–840 °C, and ultrasonic atomization—by surface extraction, tool mass balance, and before/after powder O/H/C/metal analysis. Thus the film examples and geometric ppm conversions are useful *scale estimates*, not a defensible prediction of actual contaminant concentrations or final LPBF porosity. (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000009, pqac-00000046)"}

CONTEXT. We machine powder "cups" as feedstock for a vacuum-induction ultrasonic atomizer
(AMAZEMET rePowder: graphite crucible with a BN wash, chamber pumped down then backfilled with

# Machining contamination of 6063 cups for Al–Si atomization

**Bottom line.** Published measurements show that an apparently wiped aluminum surface can retain oil at tens to roughly 150 mg/m², but they do **not** establish the residual loading after the particular IPA/Kimwipe procedure described here. For a cup having 60 cm² of exposed surface, 1 mg/m² corresponds to 6 µg per cup, or 0.12 ppm by mass in a 50 g cup. Oil is likely to outgas or decompose rather than enter the powder quantitatively; oxide, entrained solids, and some carbon- or hydrogen-bearing reaction products are more credible surviving hazards. There is no defensible published *per-cup* survival fraction for this process. (powell1995surfaceinspectionusing pages 1-2, powell1995surfaceinspectionusing pages 2-4, gobber2025productionandproperties pages 2-4)

## (a) Cutting-fluid films and wiping

An FTIR study provides **analogues, not measurements on drilled 6063**. Applying oil to aluminum foil and thoroughly wiping off the excess with *dry tissue* left approximately **150 mg/m²** (15 µg/cm²). An aluminum rod contaminated with silicone lubricant gave **49–77 mg/m²** by two spectral bands; a mineral-oil stain on sandblasted 7075 corresponded to approximately **280 mg/m²**. The same investigators reported detection of hydrocarbon films around **1 mg/m²** under favorable conditions. None of those values is an IPA-wipe endpoint or a representative distribution for an uncontrolled shop lathe. (powell1995surfaceinspectionusing pages 4-5, powell1995surfaceinspectionusing pages 7-9, powell1995surfaceinspectionusing pages 2-4, powell1995surfaceinspectionusing pages 1-2)

| Surface loading, illustrative | µg/cm² | Residue on 60 cm² cup | If divided by 50 g cup | If four cups supply 200 g melt |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 mg/m², approximately the favorable FTIR detection level | 0.10 | 6 µg | 0.12 ppm | 0.12 ppm |
| 49–77 mg/m², silicone on an aluminum rod | 4.9–7.7 | 0.294–0.462 mg | 5.9–9.2 ppm | 5.9–9.2 ppm |
| 150 mg/m², oil after *dry-tissue* wiping of foil | 15 | 0.90 mg | 18 ppm | 18 ppm |
| 280 mg/m², deliberate mineral-oil stain on 7075 | 28 | 1.68 mg | 34 ppm | 34 ppm |

The arithmetic is **total surface residue divided by metal mass**, not measured dissolved carbon, hydrogen, or final-powder concentration. For the actual charge, use the **measured** masses of the cups, plugs, and contained powder: the stated 50 g per cup and approximately 200 g per four-cup run are approximate. An estimated film thickness can also be misleading inside a blind, rough bore: pooled coolant or trapped chips need not resemble a uniform film. (powell1995surfaceinspectionusing pages 4-5, powell1995surfaceinspectionusing pages 7-9, powell1995surfaceinspectionusing pages 1-2)

**After IPA/Kimwipes:** no study retrieved measured µg/cm² remaining after that procedure on an equivalently deep aluminum bore. IPA may remove accessible, soluble oil, but wiping does not certify removal of recessed pools, dried water-soluble-coolant additives, adherent inorganic particles, or native oxide. As a useful *contrast*, optimized **distillation of 7075 chips removed 99.7% of oil and water**; that result cannot be assigned to a brief IPA wipe. Neither “zero residue” nor a particular cleaning percentage is supported for these cups. (chen2025recentadvancesin pages 4-5, powell1995surfaceinspectionusing pages 2-4, taborelli2020cleaningandsurface pages 10-12)

## (b) Tool metal, built-up edge, and shop particles

A dry-drilling study on **harder, Si-rich die-cast AlSi9Cu3**, using W6Mo5Cr4V2 HSS drills, documented adhesive, abrasive, and severe thermal wear. It measured drill-flank wear after batches of **90 holes**, but reported a normalized wear map—not a reliable drill **mass loss per hole** or Fe/W/Mo/Cr/V transferred into each workpiece. Its numerical wear-map indices must not be interpreted as milligrams of HSS in a cup. The observed material adhering to the drill was **aluminum from the workpiece**. In another Al–Si drilling study, adhered aluminum on an uncoated HSS drill reached a reported **342 mg after 49 holes**; this is aluminum *on the tool*, emphatically **not** HSS deposited in 49 parts. Neither test predicts a mass-loss rate for drilling soft 6063 with a 12.7 mm drill. (zhang2001wearmechanismmaps pages 1-2, zhang2001wearmechanismmaps pages 2-4, bhowmick2007neardrymachiningof pages 139-142, bhowmick2007neardrymachiningof pages 118-121)

WC–Co wear could introduce W and Co if a carbide turning tool chips or wears, whereas the specified HSS bore drill principally poses Fe and its actual grade-specific alloying elements; **Co is not universal to HSS**. Steel/brass swarf or particles from shared equipment can add Fe, Cu, and Zn. Aluminum-hole studies directly describe smeared metal and adhering debris; however, no applicable study retrieved quantifies WC–Co transfer, entrapped steel/brass swarf, or SiC/Al₂O₃ grit per cleaned 6063 cup. These are plausible *discrete-particle* risks, especially after filing or emery use, not justified ppm estimates. A single **1 mg** particle retained in **200 g** of charge would represent **5 ppm of that particle’s mass** if fully incorporated; its constituent-element ppm would depend on its composition and retention. Because a particle may remain as an inclusion, even a low bulk ppm need not establish LPBF acceptability. (zhang2001wearmechanismmaps pages 4-5, zhang2001wearmechanismmaps pages 2-4, bhowmick2007neardrymachiningof pages 118-121)

## (c) Altered aluminum surface

Fresh aluminum rapidly passivates; an often-reported room-temperature air-film range is **2–5 nm**. Specific Al–Mg alloy surfaces measured by XPS carried approximately **4 nm** and **7 nm** films. These are analogues, not a measured oxide thickness on this machined 6063. Water can change *chemistry as well as thickness*: aluminum micropowder film thickness was approximately **5–6 nm** in a dry/control condition and approximately **8 nm** after exposure to **95% relative humidity**, with hydroxide/OH evidence; 50% humidity did not measurably increase its thickness. Brief hydration of Al–Mg surfaces also changed their outer layer toward hydroxides. IPA wiping cannot undo that oxide. (lienhard2020surfaceoxideand pages 4-6, scottosheriff1999physicochemicalcharacterisationof pages 2-4, scottosheriff1999physicochemicalcharacterisationof pages 7-8, czech2010hydrogengenerationfrom pages 23-27)

A water-based coolant therefore adds a credible route to hydrated oxide, retained salts/additives, and localized staining **if it remains wet or dries on the metal**; it does not imply that every coolant-treated cup acquires an 8 nm film or significant corrosion. A finishing investigation describes aluminum’s approximate passive **pH 4–9** range, chloride-associated pitting, effects of copper-containing rinse water, and halo-like corrosion where coolant dries. Separately, drilling **319 Al–Si** produced a **15–20 µm** near-surface fragmentation layer in one condition and damage extending to **80 µm** with severe chip clogging. These are workpiece damage depths in a different alloy and cutting regime, **not** a measured cold-worked depth or new chemical contaminant inventory in 6063; cold work itself loses its deformed microstructure on complete melting. (bhowmick2007neardrymachiningof pages 118-121, fullen2014aluminumsurfacefinishing pages 3-7)

A simple scale calculation puts the oxide in perspective: taking **60 cm²**, a *uniform* **2–5 nm Al₂O₃** layer, density approximately **3.9 g/cm³**, and Al₂O₃ oxygen mass fraction **0.471** gives approximately **22–55 µg oxygen per cup**. If all four films’ oxygen entered a **200 g** melt, the *maximum mass-balance contribution under these assumptions* would be approximately **0.44–1.1 ppm O**. Roughness, patchy/hydrated films, other exposed surfaces, oxide removal into dross, and the powder already inside the cups invalidate this as a measured melt-O increment. The calculation underscores why a small **particle or retained coolant deposit**, rather than a pristine native film, may dominate contamination from machining. (scottosheriff1999physicochemicalcharacterisationof pages 2-4, czech2010hydrogengenerationfrom pages 23-27)

## (d) What remelting can—and cannot—remove

Pump-down favors removal of **volatile** IPA, water, and lighter hydrocarbons *provided they can escape before the sealed or tightly packed charge melts*. The small **1 mm vent** and a powder-filled, blind cavity make this a process-dependent condition, not evidence of complete degassing. Nonvolatile lubricant additives, salts, and grit will not evaporate merely because the chamber was pumped down. Upon heating, residual organics can volatilize or decompose; water and hydrated surface species can supply hydrogen through reactions with aluminum. Insoluble oxides may collect in surface dross or be entrained as films/particles; an argon backfill is not a chemical deoxidizer. Aluminum-chip recycling literature explicitly requires cutting-fluid removal and warns about gases during uncleaned remelting, but gives no IPA-wipe-to-powder survival percentage. (chen2025recentadvancesin pages 2-4, chen2025recentadvancesin pages 4-5, gobber2025productionandproperties pages 2-4)

There is **direct but non-identical feedstock-to-powder evidence**. In one vacuum-induction/argon **gas-atomization** comparison, 20–63 µm powder from Al–Si casting-alloy scrap contained **0.023 ± 0.006 wt% C**, versus **0.013 ± 0.003 wt% C** from ingot; oxygen was **0.036 ± 0.010** versus **0.049 ± 0.016 wt%**, respectively, and H was approximately **5 ppm in both**. For a *different*, modified AA2024 alloy, scrap/ingot powders contained **0.021 ± 0.005/0.011 ± 0.001 wt% C**, **0.068 ± 0.013/0.048 ± 0.013 wt% O**, and **53 ± 13/17 ± 3 ppm H**. Authors suspected scrap process fluids as one cause of elevated carbon, while noting some contamination entered slag. Starting scrap and ingot compositions differed; these are **associations, not a controlled oil-dose experiment**, and the atomizer was not this BN-washed graphite/40 kHz ultrasonic apparatus. They show why neither “vacuum removes everything” nor “all surface oil becomes carbon in powder” follows from evidence. (gobber2025productionandproperties pages 2-4, gobber2025productionandproperties pages 1-2)

Likewise, oxygen is not interchangeable with hydrogen or carbon: some oxide is separated, some can remain entrained, and fresh droplets subsequently oxidize on exposure. Hydrogen is a porosity concern because its solubility falls on solidification, while oxide films/inclusions can act as defect sites. A moisture-exposure/remelting investigation measured hydrogen increases for its specific aluminum specimens, including **0.04 ppm H** on heating commercially pure Al in air and **0.279 ppm H** for Mg-containing 5083 in air; these values are **not** predicted pickup in the present charge. Powder-processing studies provide a closer LPBF warning: AlSi10Mg reused for more than 30 months rose from roughly **0.05 to 0.12 wt% O** and **80 to 130 ppm H**, with part porosity changing from **<1% to approximately 3%** under virgin-powder-qualified parameters. In a separate, deliberately severe **400 °C/96 h air-aging** test, powder oxygen rose from **0.072 to 0.274 wt%** and manufactured-part porosity from **3.52 to 6.50%**; oxygen aging, changed laser absorption, and process behavior confound a simple causal attribution to oxygen alone. These are **powder aging/reuse**, not tests of dirty cups. (fedina2022influenceofalsi10mg pages 4-5, fiegl2021effectofalsi10mg0.4 pages 1-2, fiegl2021effectofalsi10mg0.4 pages 3-4, fedina2022influenceofalsi10mg pages 6-8, gerrard2014inclusionsandhydrogena pages 357-360)

**Carbon/carbide qualification:** a graphite/Si–Al melt study found graphite attack and carbide formation at **1500 °C** under vacuum, not at **800–840 °C** in a BN-washed crucible. It does not establish an Al₄C₃ production rate here, nor prove that residual WD-40 or cutting oil converts quantitatively to Al₄C₃. A BN wash may reduce direct graphite contact, but its actual coverage and integrity matter. Abrasive **Al₂O₃** should be treated as a possible refractory inclusion; **SiC** can remain particulate or react depending on melt contact and residence time. No retrieved measurement establishes the amount surviving this particular nozzle/sonotrode route. (hoseinpur2020mechanismsofgraphite pages 1-5)

## (e) Alloy chemistry versus powder oxygen

A published table of generally used **AA6063 compositional limits** gives **Si 0.20–0.60 wt%, Mg 0.45–0.90 wt%, Fe <0.35 wt%, Cu <0.10 wt%, Mn <0.10 wt%, and Cr <0.10 wt%**. Published AA4047 work identifies its characteristic **11–13 wt% Si**; one actual AA4047 wire contained **11.85% Si, 0.199% Fe, and 0.006% Cu**. Those **wire analyses are not AA4047 impurity limits**: the exact 4047 Fe/Cu maximum applicable to the purchased AA4047 powder should be checked against its certificate and governing specification rather than inferred from that wire. Nor do 6063 *limits* reveal the composition of the particular 6063 bar. (filippov2021microstructureandcorrosion pages 2-4, hsu2020processperformanceanalysis pages 1-3, kolubaev2022micromesoand pages 7-8)

**Most importantly, the cups are part of the charge, not just contaminated containers.** Using the question’s approximate masses, **200 g of 6063 cups/plugs** and **36–56 g of 4047 powder** would produce approximately **78–85 wt% 6063** before accounting for any other metal. Its nominal Si concentration would then be only approximately **1.9–3.5 wt%** if the 6063 contains 0.20–0.60% Si and the 4047 contains 11–13% Si—not Al–12Si. The range combines endpoints and is an arithmetic illustration, not a melt analysis. Even at the 6063 Fe ceiling, cups could contribute up to approximately **0.27–0.30 wt% Fe to the combined charge**; at its Cu ceiling, up to approximately **0.078–0.085 wt% Cu**, *before* contributions from 4047 or foreign swarf. By contrast, **1 mg** of fully incorporated pure Fe in a **200 g** run is **5 ppm Fe = 0.0005 wt%**. Bulk alloy mixing can therefore outweigh ordinary trace tool wear, while a localized steel/brass or abrasive inclusion remains a separate defect issue. If “~200 g total” instead denotes *all* metal including the 4047, reweighing each input is essential before applying those illustrative fractions. (filippov2021microstructureandcorrosion pages 2-4, hsu2020processperformanceanalysis pages 1-3, kolubaev2022micromesoand pages 7-8)

Finally, the powder’s **own surface area** is much larger than the cups’. A spherical-particle calculation for 200 g of aluminum-density material, density approximately **2.7 g/cm³** and diameter **15–45 µm**, gives approximately **10–30 m²** of powder surface, against approximately **0.024 m²** for four nominal 60 cm² cups. With a hypothetical uniform **3–5 nm Al₂O₃** shell, oxygen would be approximately **0.06–0.30 wt%** across those diameter/thickness endpoints; *not* a measured value for this Al–Si lot. Direct hot-gas-extraction data provide the better benchmark: fresh AlSi10Mg was **0.067 wt% O** in one study and approximately **0.05 wt% O** in another, whereas gas-atomized Al–Si casting-alloy powder was **0.036–0.049 wt% O** in the scrap/ingot comparison. These are **hundreds of ppm oxygen in powder**, versus the approximately **0.4–1.1 ppm O upper-bound arithmetic** for four idealized pristine cup oxides. The cup calculation must not be read as an upper bound for coolant corrosion, inclusions, air exposure during atomization, or the original **36–56 g** of 4047 powder; obtain an actual O/N/H/C analysis of both incoming and produced size fractions for this system. (fedina2022influenceofalsi10mg pages 5-6, fiegl2021effectofalsi10mg0.4 pages 3-4, fedina2022influenceofalsi10mg pages 4-5, gobber2025productionandproperties pages 2-4)

**Evidence limit:** No located publication measures the combined sequence—uncontrolled manual turning/deep HSS drilling of 6063, the stated IPA/Kimwipe wipe, BN-washed graphite melting at 800–840 °C, and ultrasonic atomization—by surface extraction, tool mass balance, and before/after powder O/H/C/metal analysis. Thus the film examples and geometric ppm conversions are useful *scale estimates*, not a defensible prediction of actual contaminant concentrations or final LPBF porosity. (chen2025recentadvancesin pages 4-5, zhang2001wearmechanismmaps pages 1-2, gobber2025productionandproperties pages 2-4)

In one vacuum-induction/argon **gas-atomization** comparison, 20–63 µm powder from Al–Si casting-alloy scrap contained **0.023 ± 0.006 wt% C**, versus **0.013 ± 0.003 wt% C** from ingot; oxygen was **0.036 ± 0.010** versus **0.049 ± 0.016 wt%**, respectively, and H was approximately **5 ppm in both**. For a *different*, modified AA2024 alloy, scrap/ingot powders contained **0.021 ± 0.005/0.011 ± 0.001 wt% C**, **0.068 ± 0.013/0.048 ± 0.013 wt% O**, and **53 ± 13/17 ± 3 ppm H**. Authors suspected scrap process fluids as one cause of elevated carbon, while noting some contamination entered slag. Starting scrap and ingot compositions differed; these are **associations, not a controlled oil-dose experiment**, and the atomizer was not this BN-washed graphite/40 kHz ultrasonic apparatus. They show why neither “vacuum removes everything” nor “all surface oil becomes carbon in powder” follows from evidence. (pqac-00000046, pqac-00000047, pqac-00000048)

Likewise, oxygen is not interchangeable with hydrogen or carbon: some oxide is separated, some can remain entrained, and fresh droplets subsequently oxidize on exposure. Hydrogen is a porosity concern because its solubility falls on solidification, while oxide films/inclusions can act as defect sites. A moisture-exposure/remelting investigation measured hydrogen increases for its specific aluminum specimens, including **0.04 ppm H** on heating commercially pure Al in air and **0.279 ppm H** for Mg-containing 5083 in air; these values are **not** predicted pickup in the present charge. Powder-processing studies provide a closer LPBF warning: AlSi10Mg reused for more than 30 months rose from roughly **0.05 to 0.12 wt% O** and **80 to 130 ppm H**, with part porosity changing from **<1% to approximately 3%** under virgin-powder-qualified parameters. In a separate, deliberately severe **400 °C/96 h air-aging** test, powder oxygen rose from **0.072 to 0.274 wt%** and manufactured-part porosity from **3.52 to 6.50%**; oxygen aging, changed laser absorption, and process behavior confound a simple causal attribution to oxygen alone. These are **powder aging/reuse**, not tests of dirty cups. (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000016, pqac-00000017, pqac-00000020, pqac-00000039, pqac-00000059)

**Carbon/carbide qualification:** a graphite/Si–Al melt study found graphite attack and carbide formation at **1500 °C** under vacuum, not at **800–840 °C** in a BN-washed crucible. It does not establish an Al₄C₃ production rate here, nor prove that residual WD-40 or cutting oil converts quantitatively to Al₄C₃. A BN wash may reduce direct graphite contact, but its actual coverage and integrity matter. Abrasive **Al₂O₃** should be treated as a possible refractory inclusion; **SiC** can remain particulate or react depending on melt contact and residence time. No retrieved measurement establishes the amount surviving this particular nozzle/sonotrode route. (pqac-00000041)

## (e) Alloy chemistry versus powder oxygen

A published table of generally used **AA6063 compositional limits** gives **Si 0.20–0.60 wt%, Mg 0.45–0.90 wt%, Fe <0.35 wt%, Cu <0.10 wt%, Mn <0.10 wt%, and Cr <0.10 wt%**. Published AA4047 work identifies its characteristic **11–13 wt% Si**; one actual AA4047 wire contained **11.85% Si, 0.199% Fe, and 0.006% Cu**. Those **wire analyses are not AA4047 impurity limits**: the exact 4047 Fe/Cu maximum applicable to the purchased AA4047 powder should be checked against its certificate and governing specification rather than inferred from that wire. Nor do 6063 *limits* reveal the composition of the particular 6063 bar. (pqac-00000054, pqac-00000061, pqac-00000063)

**Most importantly, the cups are part of the charge, not just contaminated containers.** Using the question’s approximate masses, **200 g of 6063 cups/plugs** and **36–56 g of 4047 powder** would produce approximately **78–85 wt% 6063** before accounting for any other metal. Its nominal Si concentration would then be only approximately **1.9–3.5 wt%** if the 6063 contains 0.20–0.60% Si and the 4047 contains 11–13% Si—not Al–12Si. The range combines endpoints and is an arithmetic illustration, not a melt analysis. Even at the 6063 Fe ceiling, cups could contribute up to approximately **0.27–0.30 wt% Fe to the combined charge**; at its Cu ceiling, up to approximately **0.078–0.085 wt% Cu**, *before* contributions from 4047 or foreign swarf. By contrast, **1 mg** of fully incorporated pure Fe in a **200 g** run is **5 ppm Fe = 0.0005 wt%**. Bulk alloy mixing can therefore outweigh ordinary trace tool wear, while a localized steel/brass or abrasive inclusion remains a separate defect issue. If “~200 g total” instead denotes *all* metal including the 4047, reweighing each input is essential before applying those illustrative fractions. (pqac-00000054, pqac-00000061, pqac-00000063)

Finally, the powder’s **own surface area** is much larger than the cups’. A spherical-particle calculation for 200 g of aluminum-density material, density approximately **2.7 g/cm³** and diameter **15–45 µm**, gives approximately **10–30 m²** of powder surface, against approximately **0.024 m²** for four nominal 60 cm² cups. With a hypothetical uniform **3–5 nm Al₂O₃** shell, oxygen would be approximately **0.06–0.30 wt%** across those diameter/thickness endpoints; *not* a measured value for this Al–Si lot. Direct hot-gas-extraction data provide the better benchmark: fresh AlSi10Mg was **0.067 wt% O** in one study and approximately **0.05 wt% O** in another, whereas gas-atomized Al–Si casting-alloy powder was **0.036–0.049 wt% O** in the scrap/ingot comparison. These are **hundreds of ppm oxygen in powder**, versus the approximately **0.4–1.1 ppm O upper-bound arithmetic** for four idealized pristine cup oxides. The cup calculation must not be read as an upper bound for coolant corrosion, inclusions, air exposure during atomization, or the original **36–56 g** of 4047 powder; obtain an actual O/N/H/C analysis of both incoming and produced size fractions for this system. (pqac-00000014, pqac-00000017, pqac-00000044, pqac-00000046)

**Evidence limit:** No located publication measures the combined sequence—uncontrolled manual turning/deep HSS drilling of 6063, the stated IPA/Kimwipe wipe, BN-washed graphite melting at 800–840 °C, and ultrasonic atomization—by surface extraction, tool mass balance, and before/after powder O/H/C/metal analysis. Thus the film examples and geometric ppm conversions are useful *scale estimates*, not a defensible prediction of actual contaminant concentrations or final LPBF porosity. (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000009, pqac-00000046)

contexts.context: This excerpt provides FTIR-based quantitative information for grease and oil contamination on 7075 aluminum and D6AC steel, but it does not address aluminum drilling wear, built-up edge, machining chemistry, cleaning procedures, or residual-film removal. Specimens were contaminated with Conoco HD-2 grease, Kaydol oil, and CRC silicone grease. The nominal contamination range extended from a clean step to approximately 35 mg/ft², equivalent to about 377 mg/m². The lowest explicitly reported dose was 1.5 mg/ft² CRC silicone on D6AC steel, equivalent to approximately 16.1 mg/m²; this was the only step among the six plates where contaminant presence could not be detected and distinguished from the other contaminants. Thus, the excerpt supports an approximate practical detection threshold of slightly above 16 mg/m² for that specific silicone-on-D6AC case, not a universal FTIR limit. Aluminum was more sensitive than D6AC steel. HD-2 and Kaydol were measured primarily through their 2925 cm⁻¹ C–H stretching band, while silicone used the 1265 cm⁻¹ band. HD-2 and Kaydol spectra were similar because both are aliphatic hydrocarbons, although a carbonate additive in HD-2 helped distinguish them. Averaging spectra from mapped regions improved signal-to-noise and contamination sensitivity. No cleaning-related numerical findings are present.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides quantitative results for light mineral-oil contamination on sandblasted aluminum alloy measured by reflectance FTIR. The mapped stain contained 0.54 mg of mineral oil distributed over 0.02 ft², reported as 26 mg/ft². Converting units, this is approximately 280 mg/m² (26 × 10.764). The paper’s localized extraction method used a sealed mini-conflat assembly filled with freon; shaking and recovery of the solvent removed oil from a defined plate area. A second extraction recovered 50 µg of oil, and transmission IR analysis was performed against a calibration curve prepared from the original mineral oil. The reported calibration factor was approximately 22 mg per absorbance-unit·in², while the measured stain volume was 0.0245 absorbance-unit·in². The recovered contamination estimate was about one-third of the initial spray weight gain, which may have been inflated by moisture absorption; evaporation was also possible. The excerpt does not state an explicit FTIR detection limit, cleaning endpoint, or residual-film limit. It also contains no findings from Zhang, Liu, and Zhou on HSS drilling/aluminum wear or built-up edge, nor from Brinksmeier, Mattox, or Taborelli concerning adsorbed contaminant layers and residual films. Thus, only the Powell et al. aluminum-oil contamination and solvent-extraction data can be supported here.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides comparative numerical detection information for surface-cleanliness methods, but it does not report the requested FTIR oil-contamination values in mg/m2, nor quantitative aluminum wear loss or built-up-edge data. For XPS, the listed carbon-related detection level is approximately 3 atomic percent in the probed depth, corresponding to about 10^14 atoms/cm2. XPS generally causes 10–100 times less surface damage than high-spatial-resolution AES. AES is also listed with an approximate sensitivity of 10^14 atoms/cm2, although the text warns that carbon measurements can depend on beam current density and decrease with irradiation; typical 10-second acquisitions produce doses of roughly 6×10^15 to 6×10^18 electrons/cm2. Static SIMS is identified as more chemically sensitive, with a listed carbon-species detection level of about 10^12 atoms/cm2, but interpretation and quantification are affected by matrix effects and calibration. FTIR is described as capable of detecting sub-monolayers of organic molecules, while its direct surface signal depends on roughness and it has little sensitivity to most inorganic compounds. Other listed limits include OSEE at approximately 10^15 molecules/cm2 and ellipsometry at approximately 10^12 molecules/cm2. Taborelli emphasizes that XPS yields relative atomic concentration rather than absolute molecules/cm2, and comparisons are reliable when instrument source, analyzer settings, and geometry are held constant.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides chemical-machining evidence from Brinksmeier, Lucca, and Walter, but it does not contain the requested quantitative results from Powell, Smyrl, and Williams on FTIR oil contamination in mg/m², nor the quantitative HSS-drilling aluminum wear and built-up-edge losses reported by Zhang, Liu, and Zhou. For Brinksmeier’s discussion, sulfur-containing metalworking fluids used in broad-tool finish turning of aluminum produced a tough lubricating reaction layer identified as aluminum or magnesium sulfides. The proposed mechanism is that high pressures and temperatures in the chip-formation region release sulfur from the hydrocarbon additive structure, after which sulfur reacts with the metal surface. EDX observations of chip roots showed sulfur in the chip-formation zone, while the workpiece itself contained no sulfur, supporting the interpretation that the sulfur originated in the metalworking fluid. The excerpt also describes methods relevant to adsorbed contaminants and residual films: LEED is highly surface-sensitive and requires UHV because contamination affects results; LEIS probes mainly the first monolayer; RBS can investigate near-surface composition and, with grazing incidence, depths down to 20 nm; and SIMS uses sputtering both for elemental analysis and depth profiling. No specific cleaning procedure or residual-film thickness/value from Mattox and Taborelli appears in this excerpt.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides quantitative FTIR calibration and cleaning findings, primarily for oil films on aluminum foil and contamination on galvanized sheet steel. Calibration factors for oil-related bands were: DC-200 silicone at 2965 cm⁻¹, 2.694 g m⁻² per absorbance unit (13% standard deviation); DC-200 at 1265 cm⁻¹, 1.536 g m⁻²/a.u. (17%); mineral oil at 2925 cm⁻¹, 1.491 g m⁻²/a.u. (13%); corn oil at 2925 cm⁻¹, 1.324 g m⁻²/a.u. (19%); and corn oil at 1750 cm⁻¹, 1.490 g m⁻²/a.u. (27%). The instrument noise near 2900 cm⁻¹ was approximately 0.0002 absorbance units, enabling reliable detection of hydrocarbon contamination at about 1 mg m⁻², described as a nanometer-scale film. As-received aluminum foil showed no detectable hydrocarbon bands at that noise threshold. Sulfuric-acid cleaning produced a surface condition comparable to sputter-cleaning the gold mirrors; the residual approximately 1-nm hydrocarbon film was considered equivalent to about 1 nm of carbon residue based on ESCA observations. For galvanized steel, CO₂ pellet blasting generally reduced contamination to 3–5 mg m⁻², although silicone lubricant residues of 8 and 18 mg m⁻² remained on two specimens, while uncleaned peripheral regions reached 118 mg m⁻². The excerpt contains no findings on Zhang, Liu, Zhou, Brinksmeier, Mattox, or Taborelli.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides numerical findings relevant to FTIR inspection of oil contamination on aluminum surfaces, although it does not address the requested Zhang–Liu–Zhou drilling wear or built-up-edge measurements, Brinksmeier’s machining contamination layers, or Mattox and Taborelli’s residual-film data. Reflectance FTIR is described as capable of mapping mineral, vegetable, and silicone oils and greases on aluminum and other metals. Under the best conditions, detection limits are reported in the sub-nanometer range, with excellent performance in the sub-micrometer range and useful measurement capability for films tens of microns thick. For calibration, aluminum foil was weighed, uniformly wiped with oil, thoroughly wiped with dry tissue to remove excess oil, and reweighed. This procedure typically left approximately 150 mg/m² of residue, corresponding to an approximately 150 nm film; the residue was measurable on 0.1 m² foil specimens and produced good-quality spectra. Reference gold mirrors were cleaned by degreasing with household spray cleaners containing detergents and 2-butoxyethanol, rinsing with deionized water, soaking for 1 ks in concentrated sulfuric acid, rinsing again, and rapidly drying in nitrogen. The excerpt therefore supports quantitative oil-film calibration and cleaning-procedure details, but not machined-surface wear-loss or broader adsorbed-contaminant literature findings.

contexts.question:
CONTEXT. We machine powder "cups" as feedstock for a vacuum-induction ultrasonic atomizer
(AMAZEMET rePowder: graphite crucible with a BN wash, chamber pumped down then backfilled with
argon to ~200 mbar, melt at ~800-840 C, pushed through a 0.7 mm nozzle onto a 40 kHz sonotrode),
to make Al-Si powder for laser powder bed fusion (target 15-45 um). Each cup is turned on a
shared university-shop manual lathe from 3/4 in (19.05 mm) 6063 aluminum bar: band-saw cut,
face, center drill, 1/2 in HSS twist drill 2.25 in (57 mm) deep into a blind hole, part off,
2.75 in (70 mm) long. A 6063 plug (12.9 mm dia, 14 mm long, 1 mm vent hole) is turned to a
0.0005-0.0008 in press fit. The cup is filled with 9-14 g of atomized Al-12Si (AA 4047) powder.
About four cups (~200 g total, ~60 cm2 of machined surface per cup incl. the blind bore) are
melted per run. Before filling, cups and plugs are wiped with isopropyl alcohol (IPA) on
Kimwipes and air dried. Lubricant use is not controlled: it may be dry, cutting oil, WD-40,
or a water-soluble coolant, and the lathe is shared with steel and brass work.

QUESTION 1 (machining contamination and what it does in the melt). Quantitatively, what does
lathe turning and drilling of 6xxx aluminum leave on or in the surface, and how much of it
would survive into remelted powder?
(a) Residual cutting fluid / oil / coolant film after machining, in ug/cm2 or mg/m2, and
after a solvent wipe. Convert to ppm of a ~50 g part with ~60 cm2 of surface where possible.
(b) Tool-wear debris from HSS (Fe, W, Mo, Cr, V, Co) or WC-Co tools when cutting aluminum:
wear rates or mass loss per part; built-up edge; embedded swarf or abrasive grit (SiC, Al2O3)
from shared machines, emery cloth or files.
(c) Machining-induced surface layers: oxide/hydroxide growth with water-based coolant,
staining, cold-worked layer depth.
(d) On remelting under vacuum then argon: fate of hydrocarbon and coolant residues (hydrogen
pickup and porosity, carbon or Al4C3, oxide films and bifilms, outgassing during pump-down).
Any documented effect of feedstock surface cleanliness on oxygen, hydrogen or carbon content
of gas- or ultrasonically-atomized Al alloy powder, or on LPBF porosity?
(e) Compare these levels with the composition limits of AA 6063 (e.g. Fe <= 0.35, Cu <= 0.10
wt%) and AA 4047, and with the oxygen the fine powder itself contributes (native oxide shell
on 15-45 um Al-Si powder, typical O wt%).
Give numbers with citations, and say plainly where the evidence is thin or only indirect.

contexts.context: Zhang et al. (Tribology International 34, 2001, pp. 727–731) studied uncoated HSS drilling of die-cast AlSi9Cu3. Tools were dipped in 5% NaOH to remove built-up edge; wear was measured optically at 30× with 100-µm accuracy and SEM. Dry drilling caused melting, “severe wear,” and insufficient data. Reported normalized flank-wear rates were log10(VB/L) ≈ −7.6 to −7.0 in plastic-deformation regimes and −6.7 to −6.4 in temperature-controlled regimes. Mechanisms included adhesion, Al transfer, plowing, abrasion, delamination, diffusion, plastic flow, and thermal wear. No absolute tool mass loss, debris yield, lubricant-film loading, oxide depth, hydrogen pickup, or powder/LPBF effects were provided.

contexts.context: The excerpt reports uncoated HSS drilling of die-cast aluminum, finding five mechanisms: adhesive, adhesive–abrasive, abrasive, severe plastic flow, and thermal wear. SEM showed transferred aluminum, parallel furrows, plastic distortion, ruptured edges, cracks, carbide islands, and river-bottom patterns. High temperature at the tool–work interface drives adhesion, abrasion, material transfer, diffusion, and erosion; wear “increases rapidly” in the thermal-wear region, which should be avoided. However, the excerpt supplies no numerical wear rates, debris masses, lubricant residues, contamination levels, oxide-layer depths, or remelt/atomization effects. References include Zhang et al., *Tribology International* 34 (2001) 727–731.

lathe turning and drilling of 6xxx aluminum leave on or in the surface, and how much of it
would survive into remelted powder?
(a) Residual cutting fluid / oil / coolant film after machining, in ug/cm2 or mg/m2, and
after a solvent wipe. Convert to ppm of a ~50 g part with ~60 cm2 of surface where possible.
(b) Tool-wear debris from HSS (Fe, W, Mo, Cr, V, Co) or WC-Co tools when cutting aluminum:
wear rates or mass loss per part; built-up edge; embedded swarf or abrasive grit (SiC, Al2O3)
from shared machines, emery cloth or files.
(c) Machining-induced surface layers: oxide/hydroxide growth with water-based coolant,
staining, cold-worked layer depth.
(d) On remelting under vacuum then argon: fate of hydrocarbon and coolant residues (hydrogen
pickup and porosity, carbon or Al4C3, oxide films and bifilms, outgassing during pump-down).

of gas- or ultrasonically-atomized Al alloy powder, or on LPBF porosity?
(e) Compare these levels with the composition limits of AA 6063 (e.g. Fe <= 0.35, Cu <= 0.10
wt%) and AA 4047, and with the oxygen the fine powder itself contributes (native oxide shell
on 15-45 um Al-Si powder, typical O wt%).

contexts.context: The excerpt provides surface-oxide and oxygen-distribution information for AlSi10Mg powder, but not the requested bulk oxygen weight percentages, hydrogen concentrations in ppm, humidity-dependent measurements, LPBF porosity values, or oxygen-chamber ppm. The experiments compare virgin powder (Al0) with reused/aged powders, including Al10 and Al30, using STEM-EDX and XPS before and after argon-ion etching. The virgin powder is described as having a primarily aluminum-rich oxide layer only a few nanometers thick. With aging and powder handling, the metallic Al0 signal decreases, indicating thicker oxide; Mg-containing oxide becomes increasingly prominent, particularly MgAl2O4 or MgO-related species. STEM-EDX found oxide nodules on spatter particles approximately 50–125 nm thick, with one measured nodule around 85 nm, while spatter oxide layers are described as reaching up to 120 nm. The reported oxygen profile is an XPS-derived surface-depth profile and represents a mean contribution from reused powder and spatter particles, whose proportion increases with reuse. Thus, these oxygen observations should not be interpreted as chamber oxygen concentration or bulk oxygen wt%. No AlSi12 data, hydrogen data, humidity experiment, LPBF porosity measurement, or powder-bed layer thickness is included in this excerpt.

contexts.context: The excerpt reports measured oxygen contents only for AlSi10Mg, not AlSi12. For fresh/virgin AlSi10Mg powder, oxygen was 0.067 wt% (±0.03). After processing, the R0 powder contained 0.072 wt% oxygen, indicating a slight increase. Oxygen was measured using hot-gas extraction, and the 96 h condition was selected as the worst-case aging scenario. The excerpt mentions that aluminum alloys can absorb hydrogen during storage or aging, potentially promoting pore formation, but explicitly states that no direct tendency was observed in this study and gives no hydrogen concentration in ppm. The reported before/after comparison concerns virgin powder, processed/R0 powder, and aged powder; processed powders were additionally sieved after LPBF, with an increased coarse fraction for aged material, likely due to oxygen-related melt-pool instability and spatter. Thus, oxygen wt% values are distinguishable from chamber oxygen ppm, but chamber ppm is not reported here.

contexts.context: The excerpt concerns AlSi10Mg powder degradation during laser-based powder bed fusion (LB-PBF), comparing virgin powder (Al0) with powder reused for 6, 10, 14, and 30 months (Al6, Al10, Al14, and Al30). It reports that bulk oxygen content increased with reuse time, with a sharp increase between Al0 and Al6, followed by a slower increase after six months attributed to surface passivation and formation of a stable aluminum-oxide layer. Stable Al2O3 and/or Al-Mg-oxide layers were identified as relevant oxidation products. contexts.context: The excerpt reports qualitative SEM observations of uncoated HSS drill flank wear during dry drilling of die-cast aluminum, rather than numerical flank-wear dimensions, drill mass loss, or quantified transfer volumes. At 200 mm/min feed and 4500 rev/min cutting speed, deeper parallel furrows and increased transferred aluminum indicate combined adhesive and abrasive wear. At 8000 rev/min, severe plastic distortion and plastic flow occur; deformed edges rupture and cracks form on the worn surface, attributed mainly to high tool–workpiece interface temperatures. At 10,000 rev/min, the worn surface has smooth matrix waves and carbide-particle islands resembling a river bottom. The authors identify thermal wear, including material transfer and diffusion, as the main mechanism at high speed/feed, with molten aluminum flow producing surface erosion and river-bottom-like patterns. Wear rises rapidly in this high-severity region, which should be avoided. The excerpt does not establish whether any built-up edge consists of aluminum versus tool metal, nor does it provide direct measurements of flank-wear width/depth, drill mass loss, transferred-material thickness, or embedded abrasive-particle concentration. It does, however, indicate aluminum transfer and the presence/exposure of carbide particles in the worn HSS surface.

contexts.context: The excerpt characterizes native low-temperature air-formed oxide films on Al-Mg alloys, comparing as-rolled and annealed conditions. It reports that the oxide is thicker on the annealed alloy but remains below 10 nm; it does not provide a separate numerical XPS thickness for dry versus hydrated films. Both dry native films contain oxidized magnesium, metallic-state aluminum, and aluminum- and magnesium-containing hydroxides. The annealed film has a higher magnesium content and different magnesium distribution, attributed partly to crystallized alumina and enhanced Mg diffusion. After 90 seconds of hydration, the extreme surface becomes dominated by aluminum hydroxides: XPS O1s fitting shows reduced Mg(OH)2 and Al2O3/MgO contributions, while Al2p and Mg2p indicate lower relative Mg within the analyzed depth. Magnesium oxide and hydroxide are nearly totally dissolved from the as-rolled film but are mainly imbedded in the annealed film. Hydration produces pores and cracks, with protruding hydrated oxides and Al(OH)3 crystals reported for the annealed sample. The excerpt contains no thermal-desorption OH quantification, no direct dry/hydrated thickness values derived from XPS, and no data on machined 6xxx or 319 aluminum, subsurface deformation, smeared transfer, coolant corrosion, or staining.

contexts.context: The excerpt quantifies aluminum powder passivation films using both XPS and TEM, with XPS representing an average over many particles and TEM sampling individual particles. As-received and thermally treated/dry baseline powders had smooth, uniform, fully amorphous films approximately 5–6 nm thick. Exposure to 50% relative humidity did not measurably increase film thickness, although surface roughening suggested incipient hydration. Exposure to 95% relative humidity produced a thicker film averaging approximately 8 nm, about a 45% relative increase over the control/dry condition, with larger thickness variations of roughly 3.5 nm and localized crystallinity. FTIR showed clear OH groups only for the RH-95 condition, consistent with hydration and formation of alumina oxyhydroxides. After heat treatment and vacuum desiccation (RH-95-D), the film became slightly thinner by less than 1 nm, more uniform, and showed no remaining crystallinity; the data indicate loss of hydroxide and partial recovery of a metastable oxide. The excerpt does not provide separate AlMg measurements, detailed thermal-desorption temperatures or OH quantities, nor data on machined 6xxx or 319 aluminum subsurface deformation, smeared material transfer, or coolant-corrosion staining.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides general native-oxide thickness and hydration information, but not the requested XPS measurements or quantitative data for AlMg, machined 6xxx, or 319 aluminum. On freshly exposed aluminum, the protective oxide reaches approximately 10 Å within seconds. The room-temperature air-formed film is reported as approximately 2–5 nm thick, while oxide films grown at temperatures up to 500°C can reach about 100 nm. Immersion in water thickens the film: the air-formed oxide transforms into gel-like hydroxo-complexes with an idealized composition of Al[Ox(OH)y(H2O)z]. During aging in aqueous solutions, this gelatinous material transforms sequentially into pseudo-boehmite and ultimately bayerite, Al(OH)3. At temperatures up to 80°C, bayerite and pseudoboehmite are predominant; at higher temperatures, boehmite (AlOOH) forms. The oxide is chemically hydrated/hydroxylated rather than a purely dry Al2O3/MgO film. XPS O1s fitting identified Mg(OH)2 at 531.5 eV, combined Al2O3/MgO at 532.4 eV, AlO(OH) or Al(OH)3 at 533.5 eV, and H2O/contamination at 534.6 eV. The as-rolled sample showed four O1s components, whereas the annealed alloy showed three, with water apparently desorbed during annealing. Thermal dehydration was conducted at 300 °C for 3 hours under spectrometer-chamber vacuum; the high-binding-energy hydroxide contribution was nearly eliminated, confirming its association with aluminum hydroxides. The excerpt contains no quantitative measurements of machining-induced subsurface deformation, smeared material transfer, or coolant-corrosion staining.

contexts.context: This excerpt concerns native air-formed oxide films on two cold-rolled Al-Mg alloys, not machined 6xxx or 319 aluminum. It reports a qualitative and comparative thickness result: the native oxide on the annealed A5086 alloy is twice as thick as that on the as-rolled A5182 alloy. The annealed film contains more magnesium oxide and crystalline β-Al2O3 and bayerite, whereas the as-rolled film appears amorphous. Magnesium oxide in the annealed film is less soluble in water than in the non-reheated film. Both aluminum and magnesium oxides are hydroxylated, and the surfaces behave as Brønsted bases. Water reactivity was tested by immersion in boiling deionized water for 90 seconds, and XPS was used to compare surface composition before and after hydration. However, the supplied pages do not provide numerical absolute film thicknesses, XPS-derived dry-versus-hydrated thickness values, or thermal-desorption OH measurements. They also contain no measurements of subsurface deformation, smeared material transfer, machining effects, coolant corrosion staining, or results specifically for 6xxx/319 alloys. TEM indicates that the oxide thickness is irregular, while SEM shows a non-homogeneous film with cracks exposing the substrate.

The as-rolled alloy has an amorphous oxide film, whereas annealing produces partial crystallisation and β-Al2O3/bayerite features. Hydroxide species are concentrated toward the outer surface: Mg(OH)2 is preferentially at the extreme surface, while MgO is associated with the internal interface; hydroxides are also inferred from the oxygen-rich outer region. XPS/SIMS indicate metallic aluminium within the oxide layer, attributed partly to magnesium diffusion and reduction reactions. Annealing changes magnesium distribution, producing strong external-surface enrichment, likely because crystallised alumina provides diffusion paths. The excerpt states that 90 seconds of hydration of the as-rolled sample causes pore development and cracks, but the supplied text does not quantify hydrated-film thickness or chemical changes after hydration. contexts.context: The excerpt provides direct observations from drilling a 319 aluminum-silicon alloy that are relevant to smeared or adhered material and stuck swarf in holes. As drilling progresses and the drill becomes dull through aluminum adhesion, chips clogging and built-up-edge formation increase. Type III holes, associated with a high number of drilled holes, showed large amounts of transferred aluminum, surface deterioration, and a large chunk of adhered aluminum in the chips-clogging region. This adhered material increased friction among the drill, chips, and hole wall and contributed to higher torque and a secondary torque peak. Surface roughness was worse toward the hole end, where chips jamming and BUE formation accumulated, while the entry region was relatively smoother. Metallographic examination showed a fragmentation layer approximately 15–20 µm thick in type II holes, with second-phase particles broken into 2–6 µm pieces. Type III holes exhibited substantially greater subsurface damage, with a damaged zone up to 80 µm thick; the excerpt links greater damage with increased surface roughness. It also notes that the soft aluminum matrix deforms and deposits on cutting edges, forming BUE. It does, however, provide relevant experimental evidence about hydrogen pickup and removal in molten aluminum. Hydrogen was deliberately increased by adding moist organic material to the melt; decomposition generated steam, which was absorbed by the metal. Hydrogen readings rose within a few minutes and generally stabilized after 10–15 minutes, with an initial overshoot attributed to equilibration with the furnace atmosphere. Hydrogen was subsequently reduced by purging either high-purity argon or argon containing 0.8% chlorine at 300 cc/min. In one example, measurements covered a decrease from approximately 0.35 to 0.15 ml H/100 g, representing a range typical of pre- and post-degasser readings. A preliminary pure-aluminum trial found readings varying by only ±0.01 ml/100 g over 40 minutes, while argon purging reduced hydrogen to 0.1 ml/100 g over about 50 minutes. contexts.context: The excerpt provides quantitative evidence relevant to remelting aluminum and hydrogen pickup, but it does not directly report oil burn/decomposition, bifilm populations, inclusion removal versus dissolution, BN/graphite crucible reactions, Al4C3 formation at 800–840 °C, dissolved carbon, or SiC abrasive behavior. Commercially pure aluminum develops an Al2O3 surface oxide, while Mg-containing 5083 develops MgO; the latter is described as porous and nonprotective, allowing continued reaction with atmospheric water vapor. LECO measurements removed about 85% of initial hydrogen in the first analysis and nearly all hydrogen after three analyses, leaving about 0.005 ppm. After ten weeks in laboratory air, samples reabsorbed nearly their initial hydrogen content. Moisture strongly affected uptake: after four days, 5083 absorbed 0.16 ppm in water and 0.15 ppm in laboratory air, but only 0.024 ppm in a sealed container and 0.038 ppm in acetone. Remelting experiments showed increases of 0.04 ppm H for pure Al heated in air, 0.08 ppm in nitrogen, and 0.279 ppm for 5083 heated in air. Heating caused oxide-film cracking during expansion and melting; in nitrogen, exposed aluminum surfaces formed AlN crystals in those cracks. These results support moisture- and oxide-film-related hydrogen pickup during chip remelting, while leaving the requested carbon, crucible, oil, and abrasive mechanisms undocumented here.

It explains that aluminum melt quality depends on controlling trace elements, dissolved gas, and non-metallic inclusions. Oxide skins present on charge materials can become suspended during melting and subsequently appear as massive, film-like, or dross-like inclusions. Hydrogen readily dissolves in liquid aluminum but has much lower solubility in solid aluminum, so it can generate porosity during solidification. Poor melt handling, especially violent stirring or pouring, can introduce additional oxides. Folding and entrainment of oxide-covered liquid surfaces can trap gas between oxide films, producing “double oxide film” or bifilm defects that behave like cracks. contexts.context: The excerpt provides limited but relevant evidence about remelting aluminum-based composites, particularly the behavior of SiC reinforcement. It does not report experiments on oil-covered aluminum chips, so it gives no quantitative results for oil burning or decomposition, hydrogen or water pickup, oxide bifilm formation, inclusion removal versus dissolution, carbon dissolution, or the fate of SiC used as an abrasive. It does show that SiC particles settle during remelting when the material enters the mushy zone, and that settling produces reinforcement-depleted upper melt regions with potentially large local differences in viscosity and temperature. The authors emphasize that mechanical stirring should begin as soon as the metal becomes sufficiently fluid; manual stirring is recommended beforehand and during intervals without mechanical stirring. Continuous stirring reduces SiC sedimentation, while long residence times can promote reactions between SiC and molten aluminum, reportedly forming Al4C3 (the text extraction renders this formula imperfectly) and adversely affecting melt fluidity. The study measured Al4C3 metallographically using point counting from at least four micrographs per specimen, but the supplied pages do not provide the measured values, nor do they establish formation temperatures around 800–840 °C or durations for Al12Si alloys. contexts.question:
CONTEXT. We machine powder "cups" as feedstock for a vacuum-induction ultrasonic atomizer
(AMAZEMET rePowder: graphite crucible with a BN wash, chamber pumped down then backfilled with
argon to ~200 mbar, melt at ~800-840 C, pushed through a 0.7 mm nozzle onto a 40 kHz sonotrode),
to make Al-Si powder for laser powder bed fusion (target 15-45 um). Each cup is turned on a
shared university-shop manual lathe from 3/4 in (19.05 mm) 6063 aluminum bar: band-saw cut,
face, center drill, 1/2 in HSS twist drill 2.25 in (57 mm) deep into a blind hole, part off,
2.75 in (70 mm) long. A 6063 plug (12.9 mm dia, 14 mm long, 1 mm vent hole) is turned to a
0.0005-0.0008 in press fit. The cup is filled with 9-14 g of atomized Al-12Si (AA 4047) powder.
About four cups (~200 g total, ~60 cm2 of machined surface per cup incl. the blind bore) are
melted per run. Before filling, cups and plugs are wiped with isopropyl alcohol (IPA) on
Kimwipes and air dried. Lubricant use is not controlled: it may be dry, cutting oil, WD-40,
or a water-soluble coolant, and the lathe is shared with steel and brass work.

QUESTION 1 (machining contamination and what it does in the melt). Quantitatively, what does
lathe turning and drilling of 6xxx aluminum leave on or in the surface, and how much of it
would survive into remelted powder?
(a) Residual cutting fluid / oil / coolant film after machining, in ug/cm2 or mg/m2, and
after a solvent wipe. Convert to ppm of a ~50 g part with ~60 cm2 of surface where possible.
(b) Tool-wear debris from HSS (Fe, W, Mo, Cr, V, Co) or WC-Co tools when cutting aluminum:
wear rates or mass loss per part; built-up edge; embedded swarf or abrasive grit (SiC, Al2O3)
from shared machines, emery cloth or files.
(c) Machining-induced surface layers: oxide/hydroxide growth with water-based coolant,
staining, cold-worked layer depth.
(d) On remelting under vacuum then argon: fate of hydrocarbon and coolant residues (hydrogen
pickup and porosity, carbon or Al4C3, oxide films and bifilms, outgassing during pump-down).
Any documented effect of feedstock surface cleanliness on oxygen, hydrogen or carbon content
of gas- or ultrasonically-atomized Al alloy powder, or on LPBF porosity?
(e) Compare these levels with the composition limits of AA 6063 (e.g. Fe <= 0.35, Cu <= 0.10
wt%) and AA 4047, and with the oxygen the fine powder itself contributes (native oxide shell
on 15-45 um Al-Si powder, typical O wt%).
Give numbers with citations, and say plainly where the evidence is thin or only indirect.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not provide measured carbon percentages before and after atomization, nor does it report comparative carbon, oxygen, nitrogen, or hydrogen values for scrap versus ingot feedstocks such as EN AC 46000 and AA2024. It describes only a water-atomization experiment using 1000 g of mechanically cleaned recycled aluminum scrap. The scrap was rinsed with distilled water and air-dried, but no chemical cleaning agents, flux treatments, or protective atmospheres were used. Consequently, the study did not perform a controlled cleaning or vacuum-removal experiment that could establish whether contamination was removed before atomization or whether carbon remained elevated afterward. The authors explicitly attribute potentially elevated oxygen in the powder to surface oxides and minor contaminants inherent to recycled scrap. The excerpt also does not state that vacuum treatment was used. Any comparison with EN AC 46000 or AA2024, or any conclusion that carbon increased during atomization, would therefore require data from another section or source. Chemical composition should be interpreted cautiously because the feedstock chemistry and contamination history differ, and the reported setup does not isolate the effects of atomization from those of initial scrap condition.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not report measured carbon percentages, powder-atomization scrap, ingot comparisons, EN AC 46000, or AA2024. It focuses on hydrogen absorption and removal in commercially pure aluminium and 5083 wrought alloy. Hydrogen was measured using a LECO instrument that was repeatedly outgassed at above 700°C and calibrated with pure hydrogen; repeated analysis removed nearly all measurable hydrogen, leaving approximately 0.005 ppm after three analyses. However, degassed 5083 samples later reabsorbed hydrogen when exposed to laboratory air or water, consistent with moisture-driven reaction involving its porous MgO surface. After four days, samples exposed to water and air absorbed 0.16 and 0.15 ppm H, whereas sealed and acetone-exposed samples absorbed only 0.024 and 0.038 ppm. Separate furnace experiments measured hydrogen uptake after heating pure aluminium or 5083 in air or nitrogen, with increases of 0.04, 0.08, and 0.279 ppm respectively. The excerpt therefore provides limited contextual evidence about hydrogen degassing, atmospheric reabsorption, and effects of oxide/nitride surface films, but contains no carbon data or controlled cleaning comparison relevant to the requested alloy and atomization study.

contexts.context: The provided excerpt does not include the measured carbon, oxygen, nitrogen, or hydrogen percentages before and after atomization for scrap versus ingot EN AC 46000 and AA 2024. It also does not report whether vacuum treatment removed contamination, whether carbon remained elevated after atomization, or provide results from a controlled cleaning experiment. The relevant conclusion is that powders made from ingot and industrial scrap had comparable overall quality, but scrap alloys showed minor variations in light-element content that may result from contamination by process fluids. For AA 2024, the different flowability of scrap and ingot powders was not explained by particle morphology or particle-size distribution. The authors suggest that differences in chemical composition and surface properties—possibly involving Mg and thin surface oxides—could influence particle friction and processability. Therefore, any comparison of carbon or other light elements should be made cautiously: the scrap and ingot feedstocks may have differed chemically before atomization, and the excerpt does not establish that atomization or vacuum processing alone caused the observed changes. The article explicitly indicates that further chemical characterization is needed, so it should not be interpreted as a controlled demonstration that cleaning or vacuum processing removed contamination.

Thus, vacuum melting appears to remove or reduce some contamination, but carbon remains higher in scrap-derived powder. Comparisons require caution because the alloys differ chemically, especially the Ti-containing modified AA 2024, which is linked to higher nitrogen and hydrogen. The excerpt reports observations rather than a controlled cleaning experiment, so it does not establish the independent effect of vacuum cleaning.

contexts.context: The excerpt is only partially relevant to the requested comparison of published AA6063 and AA4047 composition limits. It does not state the formal AA6063 upper limits (Fe 0.35, Cu 0.10, Mg 0.45–0.9, Si 0.2–0.6, Cr 0.10, Mn 0.10) or the formal AA4047 limits (Fe ≤0.8, Cu ≤0.3, Si 11–13). It also does not provide a standards-based distinction between nominal/formal alloy limits and measured product composition. Instead, the paper reports local, experimentally measured composition and phases in an AA4047/AA7075 additively manufactured wall and transition zone. EDS profiles show Mg, Zn, and Cu decreasing sharply through the transition zone while Si increases. The deposited AA4047 region contains α-Al and Al/Si eutectic structures, with some Fe-Si-Al-related phases. The transition zone contains intermixed alloy material and locally measured Mg levels up to 2.5 at.%, while XRD identifies α-Al, Si, and MgZn2. These values describe the particular deposited material and spatially varying microstructure; they should not be treated as certification of AA4047 composition limits or as a substitute for a published chemical-composition specification.

contexts.question:
CONTEXT. We machine powder "cups" as feedstock for a vacuum-induction ultrasonic atomizer
(AMAZEMET rePowder: graphite crucible with a BN wash, chamber pumped down then backfilled with
argon to ~200 mbar, melt at ~800-840 C, pushed through a 0.7 mm nozzle onto a 40 kHz sonotrode),
to make Al-Si powder for laser powder bed fusion (target 15-45 um). Each cup is turned on a
shared university-shop manual lathe from 3/4 in (19.05 mm) 6063 aluminum bar: band-saw cut,
face, center drill, 1/2 in HSS twist drill 2.25 in (57 mm) deep into a blind hole, part off,
2.75 in (70 mm) long. A 6063 plug (12.9 mm dia, 14 mm long, 1 mm vent hole) is turned to a
0.0005-0.0008 in press fit. The cup is filled with 9-14 g of atomized Al-12Si (AA 4047) powder.
About four cups (~200 g total, ~60 cm2 of machined surface per cup incl. the blind bore) are
melted per run. Before filling, cups and plugs are wiped with isopropyl alcohol (IPA) on
Kimwipes and air dried. Lubricant use is not controlled: it may be dry, cutting oil, WD-40,
or a water-soluble coolant, and the lathe is shared with steel and brass work.

QUESTION 1 (machining contamination and what it does in the melt). Quantitatively, what does
lathe turning and drilling of 6xxx aluminum leave on or in the surface, and how much of it
would survive into remelted powder?
(a) Residual cutting fluid / oil / coolant film after machining, in ug/cm2 or mg/m2, and
after a solvent wipe. Convert to ppm of a ~50 g part with ~60 cm2 of surface where possible.
(b) Tool-wear debris from HSS (Fe, W, Mo, Cr, V, Co) or WC-Co tools when cutting aluminum:
wear rates or mass loss per part; built-up edge; embedded swarf or abrasive grit (SiC, Al2O3)
from shared machines, emery cloth or files.
(c) Machining-induced surface layers: oxide/hydroxide growth with water-based coolant,
staining, cold-worked layer depth.
(d) On remelting under vacuum then argon: fate of hydrocarbon and coolant residues (hydrogen
pickup and porosity, carbon or Al4C3, oxide films and bifilms, outgassing during pump-down).
Any documented effect of feedstock surface cleanliness on oxygen, hydrogen or carbon content
of gas- or ultrasonically-atomized Al alloy powder, or on LPBF porosity?
(e) Compare these levels with the composition limits of AA 6063 (e.g. Fe <= 0.35, Cu <= 0.10
wt%) and AA 4047, and with the oxygen the fine powder itself contributes (native oxide shell
on 15-45 um Al-Si powder, typical O wt%).
Give numbers with citations, and say plainly where the evidence is thin or only indirect.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides no quantitative evidence on lathe-fluid residues, tool wear, embedded debris, oxide layers, hydrogen/carbon pickup, or aluminum powder oxygen content. It discusses EBAM rather than ultrasonic atomization or remelting cups. Relevant indirect findings are that insufficient remelting leaves shrinkage cavities and gas pores; excessive heat input causes magnesium evaporation and large gas pores. For AA5356, optimized heat input reduced porosity from 0.8% to 0.2%, average pore size from 4 to 1 μm, and minimized magnesium loss. These results concern printed Al-Mg alloy and cannot establish contamination levels for Al-Si feedstock.
